text.fr:
À Mattoon (Ill.). À Mattoon, des observations ont été faites par le professeur G. M. Hough, de l'Observatoire Dudley, Albany, New York ; David Murry, de Rutgers College, New Brunswick (N. J.), et d'autres. Les instruments utilisés étaient des télescopes ordinaires. À quatre heures dix minutes et quinze secondes l'éclipse a commencé, le premier contact de la Lune avec le Soleil se produisant quand la première se trouvait à 19 degrés au sud de l'équateur solaire, du côté ouest. Le thermomètre, qui quelques instants auparavant était monté à 102 degrés, a commencé à baisser rapidement. À 5 heures 11 minutes et 17 secondes le Soleil a été totalement obscurci. L'obscurité égalait celle d'une nuit de clair de lune et la température était inférieure de 42 degrés à celle d'une heure auparavant. L'éclipse a pris fin à 6 heures 9 min. et 22 sec. Dans les observations faites, les phénomènes ont correspondu exactement aux calculs précédemment établis. Six taches étaient visibles à la surface du Soleil avant l'éclipse, dont deux très en vue et les autres beaucoup moins. Les cornes de la Lune avaient un aspect déchiqueté et flou. À mesure que l'éclipse progressait vers la totalité, la forme de la Lune est devenue visible près des cornes des phénomènes de la totalité. Les « grains de Baily » ont été vus distinctement par tous les observateurs, s'étendant sur un arc d'au moins 50 degrés. Les protubérances en forme de flammes ont été vues avec une netteté merveilleuse, une très grande sur le bord inférieur du Soleil et trois presque aussi grandes sur le bord supérieur, tandis qu'au moins sept ou huit en tout étaient visibles. Celle du bord droit ou inférieur avait quelque peu l'aspect d'un navire gréé, toutes voiles dehors. Dans sa partie la plus proche de la Lune se trouvaient deux ou trois taches d'un noir de jais. À l'œil nu, il semblait y avoir des ouvertures dans la Lune—deux de chaque côté et une du côté sud-ouest.

Juste après l'éclipse totale, à travers l'ouverture, la lueur sinistre du Soleil était distinctement visible. La couronne n'était pas telle qu'on la décrit généralement dans les livres, avec un halo de lumière entourant la Lune, mais avait nettement la forme de cinq pointes en fourche sur le pourtour inférieur et de deux pointes sur le pourtour supérieur de la Lune. Ces pointes présentaient un aspect rayonnant. La théorie généralement reçue au sujet de cette couronne, selon laquelle elle serait l'atmosphère du Soleil, ne paraît pas confirmée par les observations faites en ce point. On conjecture que la couronne est d'une façon ou d'une autre causée par le phénomène de la lumière traversant l'atmosphère. Bien qu'on ait cherché, aucun corps planétaire n'a été observé entre Mercure et le Soleil. Pendant la phase de totalité, Mercure, Vénus, Régulus, Mars, Saturne, Denebola et d'autres étoiles étaient visibles. La température à l'ombre au début de l'éclipse était de 77 degrés, pendant la totalité de 45 degrés et à la fin de l'éclipse elle était remontée à 70 degrés. À 3.40 heures, sous le soleil, sur l'herbe, le thermomètre était à 100 ; quelques minutes après 4 heures il était à 102, tandis que pendant l'éclipse totale il est tombé à 60 degrés, mais est ensuite remonté à 80 degrés.
text.es:
En Mattoon, Ill. En Mattoon hicieron observaciones el profesor G. M. Hough, del Observatorio Dudley, de Albany, Nueva York; David Murry, del Rutgers College, de New Brunswick, N. J., y otros. Los instrumentos empleados fueron telescopios corrientes. A las cuatro y diez minutos y quince segundos comenzó el eclipse, produciéndose el primer contacto de la Luna con el Sol cuando la primera estaba a 19 grados al sur del ecuador solar, en el lado oeste. El termómetro, que unos momentos antes había subido a 102 grados, empezó a bajar rápidamente. A las 5 y 11 minutos y 17 segundos el Sol quedó totalmente oscurecido. La oscuridad era igual a la de una noche de luna y la temperatura era 42 grados más fría que una hora antes. El eclipse terminó a las seis y 9 min. y 22 seg. En las observaciones realizadas los fenómenos concordaron exactamente con los cálculos hechos previamente. Antes del eclipse eran visibles seis manchas en la superficie del Sol, dos de las cuales eran muy prominentes y las otras mucho menos. Las puntas de la Luna tenían un aspecto irregular y borroso. A medida que el eclipse avanzaba hacia la totalidad, la forma de la Luna se hizo visible cerca de las puntas de los fenómenos de la totalidad. Las «perlas de Baily» fueron vistas con claridad por todos los observadores, extendiéndose a lo largo de un arco de al menos 50 grados. Las protuberancias en forma de llama se vieron con una nitidez maravillosa, una muy grande en el límite inferior del Sol y tres casi tan grandes en el límite superior, mientras que eran visibles en total al menos siete u ocho de ellas. La de la mano derecha o limbo inferior tenía algo del aspecto de un buque de aparejo completo con las velas desplegadas. En su parte más próxima a la Luna había dos o tres manchas negro azabache. A simple vista parecía como si hubiera aberturas en la Luna — dos a cada lado y una en el lado sudoeste.

Justo después del eclipse total, a través de la abertura se veía claramente el resplandor lívido del Sol. La corona no era como se describe generalmente en los libros, con un halo de luz que rodea la Luna, sino que tenía claramente la forma de cinco puntas agudas en la circunferencia inferior y dos puntas en la superior de la Luna. Estas puntas presentaban un aspecto radiante. La teoría generalmente aceptada acerca de esta corona, según la cual es la atmósfera del Sol, no parece quedar sustentada por las observaciones hechas en este punto. Se conjetura que la corona está causada de algún modo por los fenómenos de la luz al atravesar la atmósfera. Aunque se buscó, no se observó ningún cuerpo planetario entre Mercurio y el Sol. Durante la fase de totalidad fueron visibles Mercurio, Venus, Régulo, Marte, Saturno, Denébola y otras estrellas. La temperatura a la sombra al comienzo del eclipse era de 77 grados, durante la totalidad de 45 grados y al final del eclipse había subido a 70 grados. A las 3.40, bajo el sol, sobre la hierba el termómetro marcaba 100; pocos minutos después de las 4 marcaba 102, mientras que durante el eclipse total bajó a 60 grados, pero posteriormente subió a 80 grados.
text.it:
A Mattoon, Ill. A Mattoon le osservazioni sono state fatte dal professor G. M. Hough, del Dudley Observatory di Albany, New York; da David Murry del Rutgers College di New Brunswick, N. J., e da altri. Gli strumenti utilizzati erano comuni telescopi. Alle quattro e dieci minuti e quindici secondi è cominciata l'eclissi, con il primo contatto della Luna con il Sole avvenuto quando la prima si trovava a 19 gradi a sud dell'equatore solare sul lato occidentale. Il termometro, che pochi istanti prima era salito a 102 gradi, ha cominciato a scendere rapidamente. Alle 5 e 11 minuti e 17 secondi il Sole è stato totalmente oscurato. L'oscurità era pari a quella di una notte al chiaro di luna e la temperatura era di 42 gradi più fredda di un'ora prima. L'eclissi è finita alle sei e 9 min. e 22 sec. Nelle osservazioni effettuate i fenomeni hanno corrisposto esattamente ai calcoli fatti in precedenza. Sei macchie erano visibili sulla superficie del Sole prima dell'eclissi, due delle quali molto evidenti e le altre molto meno. Le cuspidi sulla Luna avevano un aspetto frastagliato e sfocato. Man mano che l'eclissi procedeva verso la totalità la forma della Luna è diventata visibile presso le cuspidi dei fenomeni della totalità. I «grani di Bailey» sono stati visti distintamente da tutti gli osservatori, estesi su un arco di almeno 50 gradi. Le protuberanze simili a fiamme sono state viste con meravigliosa nitidezza, una molto grande sul bordo inferiore del Sole e tre quasi altrettanto grandi sul bordo superiore, mentre in tutto ne erano visibili almeno sette o otto. Quella sul lato destro o bordo inferiore aveva un po' l'aspetto di una nave a vele spiegate con tutto l'attrezzo. Nella sua parte più vicina alla Luna c'erano due o tre macchie nere come il giaietto. A occhio nudo sembrava che ci fossero aperture nella Luna, due da ciascun lato e una sul lato sud-ovest.

Subito dopo l'eclissi totale, attraverso l'apertura, il bagliore livido del Sole era distintamente visibile. La corona non era come generalmente descritta nei libri, con un alone di luce attorno alla Luna, ma aveva distintamente la forma di cinque rebbi appuntiti sulla circonferenza inferiore e di due rebbi su quella superiore della Luna. Queste punte presentavano un aspetto radiante. La teoria generalmente accettata riguardo a questa corona, che essa sia l'atmosfera del Sole, non sembra confermata dalle osservazioni fatte in questo punto. Si congettura che la corona sia in qualche modo causata dal fenomeno della luce che passa attraverso l'atmosfera. Benché siano state fatte ricerche, non sono stati osservati corpi planetari tra Mercurio e il Sole. Durante la fase della totalità erano visibili Mercurio, Venere, Regolo, Marte, Saturno, Denebola e altre stelle. La temperatura all'ombra all'inizio dell'eclissi era di 77 gradi, durante la totalità di 45 gradi e alla fine dell'eclissi era salita a 70 gradi. Alle 3.40, sotto il sole, sull'erba, il termometro era a 100; pochi minuti dopo le 4 era a 102, mentre durante l'eclissi totale è sceso a 60 gradi, ma successivamente è salito a 80 gradi.
text.ja:
イリノイ州マトゥーンにて。マトゥーンでは、ニューヨーク州オールバニのダドリー天文台のG・M・ハフ教授、ニュージャージー州ニューブランズウィックのラトガース・カレッジのデイヴィッド・マリーらによって観測が行われた。用いられた器械は通常の望遠鏡であった。4時10分15秒に日食が始まり、月が太陽に最初に接したのは、月が太陽の赤道の南19度、西側にあるときであった。その少し前に102度まで上がっていた温度計は、急速に下がり始めた。5時11分17秒に、太陽は完全に隠された。暗さは月夜のそれに等しく、気温は1時間前より42度低かった。日食は6時9分22秒に終わった。行われた観測では、現象は先にされていた計算と正確に一致した。食の前、太陽の表面には6つの黒点が見え、そのうち2つはきわめて目立ち、残りはずっと目立たなかった。月の尖端はぎざぎざで、ぼやけた様子をしていた。食が皆既に向かって進むにつれて、皆既の現象の尖端付近に月の形が見えるようになった。「ベイリー・ビーズ」は観測者全員にはっきりと見え、少なくとも50度の弧にわたって広がっていた。炎のような紅炎は驚くほどはっきりと見え、太陽の下の縁には非常に大きなものが1つ、上の縁にはそれとほぼ同じ大きさのものが3つあり、全部で少なくとも7つか8つが見えた。右手すなわち下の縁にあるものは、帆を張った全装の帆船にいくらか似た姿をしていた。月に最も近い部分には、真っ黒な斑点が2つか3つあった。肉眼には、月に開口部があるかのように見えた—両側に2つずつ、南西側に1つである。

皆既日食の直後、その開口部を通して、太陽のぎらつく輝きがはっきりと見えた。コロナは、書物に一般に述べられているような、月を取り巻く光の暈ではなく、はっきりと、月の下の周に5本、上の周に2本の尖った叉の形をしていた。これらの先端は放射状の様相を呈していた。このコロナについて一般に受け入れられている説、すなわちそれが太陽の大気であるという説は、この地点で行われた観測によっては支持されないように思われる。コロナは、光が大気を通過する現象によって何らかの形で生じるのではないかと推測されている。探索は行われたものの、水星と太陽の間に惑星の類は観測されなかった。皆既の間には、水星、金星、レグルス、火星、土星、デネボラ、その他の星が見えた。日陰の気温は、日食の始まりには77度、皆既の間には45度であり、日食の終わりには70度まで上がっていた。3時40分には、草地の日なたで温度計は100度を示し、4時を数分過ぎると102度になったが、皆既日食の間には60度まで下がり、その後80度まで上がった。

text_orig:
It is not often that an opportunity is offered to witness so wonderful an exhibition of nature as the eclipse of Saturday last. Those who witnessed this extraordinary spectacle intelligently, will never forget its impression. It excites the most lively feelings of awe and wonder, and a breathless intensity takes possession of one as he gazes upon this grand movement in the heavens. The sight certainly gives one, a clearer view of the infinite majesty and power of the Great Being, and seems to speak directly to us of His greatness. The day was favorable, the forenoon was slightly hazy, but it cleared away and left no obstruction while the eclipse was passing.

The parties of observations were quite successful. Cedar Falls was made one of the points of observation by the Government, and will hereafter be one of the points from which calculations will be made. The party sent out by the Government to take observations in this city were Ed. W. Horr, son of Dr. Horr of the Smithsonian Institute, and Wm. I. Anderson and W. W. Wormood, of Dubuque.

We publish below their report, which we clip from the Dubuque Herald, also the observations made by a party composed of our citizens. The two reports give a full description of all that can be given concerning this great event.

THE REPORT.

DUBUQUE, Aug. 9, 1869.

To the President of the Iowa Institute of Science and Arts:

Dear Sir:—In compliance with your request we visited Cedar Falls, Iowa, on the 7th inst., to make observation upon the duration of the total phase of the eclipse of the sun. We were provided with five double and single quarter second watches, which were generously furnished for the purpose by Messrs. Giles, Morse & Co., of this place. We were kindly assisted by George C. Dean, of Dubuque, and J. H. Stanley and J. J. Tolerton, of Cedar Falls, who took stations as observers. The line of observation and the positions of the observers were located by E. Rodenberger, civil engineer, who also gratuitously furnished an accurate plat of the same, which is herewith presented. At 12 o'clock noon, we corrected the watches by the signals transmitted by telegraph of the precise mean time of Dubuque.

The first station was half a mile northeast of the Soldiers' Orphans' Home, which is two miles south of the city; the second at the cupola of the Orphans' Home; the third, fourth and fifth, on the same line, half a mile apart extending southwest.

In due time the stations were occupied—the first by Geo. C. Dean; second, by E. W. Horr; third, by W. W. Wormood; fourth, by J. J. Tolerton, and the fifth by Wm. I. Anderson. In addition an observation was made by J. H. Stanley, opposite his store on Main street. Each of whom were provided with colored glasses, lantern and assistants.

The sky, which had been clear during the day, became slightly hazy a short time before the beginning of the eclipse, but which did not in any respect interfere with the perfection of the observation. The wind blew all day a gentle breeze from the east.

At the store of Wise & Bryant the average temperature in the shade, before the eclipse, was 74 degrees, which at the period of totality fell to 67 degrees.

At the Orphans' Home the first contact was at 3 o'clock, 53 minutes and 9½ seconds; last contact 5 o'clock, 53 minutes and 42 seconds. Duration, 2 hours, 32½ seconds.

Total phase lasted 63¾ seconds, with a variation from 71 seconds at one and a half miles southeast of the Orphans' Home to 51 seconds in the city. The corona was well defined. The moments of immersion and emersion of the sun were startlingly instantaneous, and were of such thrilling interest to behold as to require no ordinary power of attention to secure accuracy in recording the period of duration. During the time dew deposited plentifully on the grass.

At the southwest the darkness was of the blackest character, while at the northeast, through a lurid haze, trees could be seen basking in the dim sunlight, in the vicinity of Janesville, eight or ten miles distant.

This was the most wonderful natural phenomenen ever witnessed by the citizens of Cedar Falls, and of more interest than any that will be observed there in the present century.

Acknowledgments are due to Supt. Farley for passes over the railroad and to the telegraph agents for the free use of the lines.

OBSERVATIONS FROM RESIDENCE OF D. C. OVERMAN, ESQ.

Mr. Editor:—The writer, in company with Messrs. D. C. and J. M. Overman and Mr. Wild, who has recently returned from Germany, was permitted to view and take observations of the eclipse of last Saturday, from the top of the new residence of D. C. Overman, Esq. We had chosen for our point of observation one of the highest in Black Hawk county, where we could get a full view of Cedar Falls and the surrounding country. From the elevated position selected, we could count four hundred distinct farm houses, and could discover objects in five counties, viz: Black Hawk, Grundy, Butler, Bremer and Buchanan. It is claimed, also, that in favorable and clear weather, the woods near Independence, thirty miles off, could be seen with the naked eye. We had made ample preparation for the rich treat, posting ourselves on the notes taken by persons who had seen similar eclipses before, and had provided ourselves with colored and smoked glass, good time pieces, stop watches, &c. Our time was taken from the party sent to Cedar Falls by the Government to make observations. Cedar Falls was so near the northern limit, that we had the advantage of the total as well as the sublime sight beyond the north limit.

We could see the sunlight on distant parts of the landscape, being involved in the total, and could also see the light shining on the land in the distant horizon 20 or 30 miles off, as the mighty shadow swept on to the east.

Our party all agreed that the first appearance was seen at precisely 3:54, just the time our Government party said it would begin, and by having the exact time of the astronomical watches, we could tell just what time to look for it.

As before stated, it first made its appearance at three o'clock and fifty four seconds, and was just two hours to a second to the end of the eclipse. Beginning of totality, four o'clock and fifty-three minutes; end of totality, four o'clock fifty-three minutes and fifty-eight seconds, which would make the total eclipse just 58 seconds.

When the sun was about half hidden by the dark disk of the moon, our attention was called to the appearance of the sky in the north, a gloom was thrown on all the landscape, and the sky was of a deep dense, black blue, particularly the horizon as if a terrible storm was approaching. The trees in the distant had lost their lively verdure, the golden wheat fields had a dull sickly color, and gradual approach of darkness became impressive. The sun light on the south and southeast had become much weakend, it had that unearthly greenish and reddish gloomy, sickly, faint, aspect making the contrast between the sky in the north and south very great. It appeared as if the sky was descending to the ground and the horizon contracting. As we could see for miles to the north and east, the sight was grand, beautiful, inspiring awe and wonder.

As the eclipse advanced to within a few seconds of the total observation, the scene became intensly interesting, particularly at the north. The big woods and the timber in the valley of the Cedar had lost their beautiful verdure and looked like outlines of dark pictures in an unfamiliar country. It was a magnificent sight, not quite as dark as night, but it appeared as if the sky at the horizon was putting on a deep blue black; the sky to the south, near the horizon, was of a brownish yellow.

As the totality appeared, a breathless intensity of interest was manifest by all of our party, and all nature seemed hushed, and as Cooper describes the eclipse of 1806: "all living creatures seemed thrown into a state of agitation; the doves and martins returned to boxes, birds were fluttering to and fro, butterflies fell to the ground in a state of stupor, the singing of the birds became hushed, the fowls went to roost, and within a minute of the total darkness, the sun appeared like a thin crescent, line becoming more and more broken up as it advances," I suppose owing to the irregular edge of the moon and its mountains.

We look around us now on the countenances of those of our party, all wear a look of wonder and anxiety, watching for the approach of the moon's shadow. Suddenly one of the party shouted, there it is—the "shadow!" The awful shadow of the moon was approaching us at a velocity of a mile a second, from the west, as a dark, vast mass, or column, or cloud, as the description had been given us. How grand this sight was, as the mighty shadow swept onward to the east.

The approach and recession of the shadow was not uniform, but dark stripes appeared fluttering across the landscape and the edges appeared tremulous, and one of our party, who was looking at the eclipse just as the last visible ray disappeared, says it is like a flicker of a candle going out. It seemed but a second before we were immersed in the shadow, and as near as we could calculate, the shadow was 30 to 40 seconds passing over, from the time when first seen until it had passed away.

Now comes the grand sight—in an instant the panorama is changed, the dark clouds that were at the north changed positions to the south, which was as black as the darkness of night. To the north and northeast, say one third of the horizon as we could scan with the eye, we could see plainly, objects beyond the disk on the distant landscape. All above is of a deep blue or black, to the south and southwest a deep jet black, while at the north a mellow, faint, yellowish or brimstone color and beautiful, the wheat fields waving with the golden grain, the varied hues of green, with the white farm houses doted here and there, appeared. Above us now was the twinkling stars, glittering in all their glory, in the broad dark zone—night, with the stars above us, to south and west of us, and to the north and east of us, 10 or 12 miles, Old Sol shining on the landscape—and the dark, deep shadow sleeping on the southwest in all of its blackness. What a variety of views we can take in with one scanning of the eye. Around and over us, we can't describe it. At this moment, we have to the southeast, south and west, the blackness of a terrible storm, to the north the distant objects have a fine yellow hue, and to the east a fine purple hue, and the deep blue overhead, with stars peeping out, with the sun entirely hid, with the beautiful, faint crown of light apparently surrounding the moon, with the faint streaks like jets of flame are seen protruding from the edge, the coolness was great, as the themometer had fallen some twenty degrees.

As Cooper says: "there was breathless intensity of gloom" manifested by all of our party, and there should be a feeling of something instructive in this awful phenomena, and one of humiliation and awe. The sight was certainly much finer from our point of observation than farther to the center, for we had the effect of the totality a sufficient length of time to get the full benefit of it, with the adition of seeing the sunlight on the distant parts of the landscape beyond the northern boundary, and as the restoration begun, the landscape became more beautiful, the striking contrast of the glorious and sublime spectacle of the light on the distant landscape as it began to play among the golden fields and the distant hills and forests, it were as if a flood of grateful and cheering brightness had fallen into the Cedar Valley, with a sweet mellow tinge and power beyond description. It was sudden and amazing change from the dark, gloomy appearance of a few moments before. From the south, where now all was dark, the contrast was great, and Cooper, in his description of the eclipse in 1806, describes the appear- of the eclipse of last Saturday better than I can:

I can liken this sudden, joyous return of light, after the eclipse, to nothing of the kind that is familiarly known. It was certainly nearest to the change produced by the swift passage of the shadow of a very dark cloud, but it was the effect of this instantaneous transition, multiplied more than a thousand fold. It seemed to speak directly to our spirits, with assurance of protection, of gracious mercy, and that Divine love which has produced all the glorious combinations of matter for our enjoyment. It was not in the least like the gradual dawning of day, or the actual rising of the sun. There was no gradation in the change. It was sudden, amazing, like what the imagination would teach us to expect of the advent of a heavenly vision. I know that philosophically I am wrong; but, to me, it seems that the rays might actually be seen floating through the darkness in torrents, till they had again illuminated the forest, the mountains, the valley, and the lake with their glowing, genial touch.

Mr. Editor, it cannot be described, and I will not attempt it further. I will recapitulate:

We are in about 42° 33′ of Latitude and 92° 27′ of Longitude. Beginning of the eclipse, 3 o'clock and fifty-four minutes; beginning of the totality, 4 o'clock fifty-three minutes; end of the totality, 4 o'clock, fifty-three minutes and fifty-eight seconds; end of the eclipse, 5 o'clock fifty-three minutes and thirty seconds. Time of passing of the shadow, forty seconds.

We were located about one mile north of the Orphans' Home, where the Government party took their observations, and our time nearly corresponded with theirs.
