Ricordai che a meno di cento miglia da me vi sarebbe stata solo un'eclissi parziale, e che in una stretta fascia larga centoquaranta miglia, i cui limiti erano stati determinati con la stessa accuratezza dei confini dei campi di un uomo, ero venuto a vedere un'eclissi totale. Anzi, ancora di più. Mi trovavo il più vicino possibile alla linea centrale esatta di questa eclissi totale.

Se l'astronomia ha un futuro, ha anche un passato. Se c'è ancora molto da imparare, qualcosa è già stato ottenuto. Accanto a me stava uno spettroscopio, quel meraviglioso strumento con cui non solo il nostro Sole, ma i soli di altri sistemi dovranno essere conosciuti con la stessa accuratezza, e i loro elementi costituenti determinati con la stessa precisione dell'acqua che scorreva ai miei piedi.

Mentre la Luna procedeva nella sua solenne marcia, ogni lavoro fu sospeso. Gli strumenti che non erano in posizione esatta furono lasciati com'erano. Perché ogni momento diventava prezioso. Il nostro gruppo non era un gruppo scientifico, e dovevamo usare i nostri occhi, e dipendere da altre fonti per la conoscenza scientifica. Perfino quelli che erano stati assorbiti dal racconto che Fenimore Cooper diede della grande eclissi del 1806 smisero di leggere. Potevano leggere quel bel racconto in qualsiasi momento. Solo una volta, e questa era ora, potevano vedere essi stessi.

Man mano che l'oscuramento aumentava, vi fu un marcato cambiamento della temperatura. Non credo che molti di noi si aspettassero una differenza così grande. Un termometro in possesso del signor Robert Brown, Jr., fu esposto alla luce solare, e a lui devo le informazioni relative al cambiamento della posizione del mercurio. Alle 4:50 era indicata una temperatura di 89°. Alle 4:55:30 di 91°. A questo punto rimase stazionario fino alle 5. In quel momento cominciò a scendere gradualmente. Alle 5:05 era a 88°. Alle 5:10 a 86°. Da quel momento in poi la sua discesa fu più rapida, ed è indicata dalla tabella seguente:

Ora. | Gradi. | Ora. | Gradi.
5:11 | 83,40 | 5:21 | 79,40
5:12 | […] | 5:2[…]½ | 79
5:13 | 84 | 5:23 | 78,30
5:14 | 83,40 | 5:24 | 78
5:15 | 83,30 | 5:25 | 77,20
5:16 | 82,20 | 5:26 | 77
5:17 | 82 | 5:27 | 76,30
5:18 | 81,20 | 5:28 | […]
5:19 | […] | 5:29 | 74,80
5:20 | 80,30 |  | 

All'ora più tarda, le 5:29, cominciò l'oscuramento, e continuò per due minuti e dieci secondi. Alle 5:31:10 il mercurio indicava una temperatura di 73°. Così, in meno di una sola ora, il mercurio era sceso di 18°. Nei due minuti e dieci secondi di oscuramento totale era sceso di un grado e mezzo.

Fu quando circa un terzo del disco del Sole era oscurato che alcuni pensarono di poter distinguere un cambiamento nella luce. Sembrava avere una sfumatura grigiastra che prima non era stata notata. Quando la Luna fu a metà strada, la forma a falce del Sole cominciò ad attirare l'attenzione generale, e allora non ci fu nessuno che non vedesse una diminuzione della luce. Lo si poteva vedere specialmente nel suo riflesso dalle acque. Poiché, mentre le onde erano state così scintillanti alla luce del sole da abbagliare e accecare gli occhi di chi guardava, ora su di esse stava un'opacità, come se il Sole splendesse attraverso un sottile velo di nubi. Era notevole anche che i grandi avvoltoi—uccelli di malaugurio—che avevano volato alti nell'aria, ora volteggiassero a un livello più basso. Proprio allora anche un vento venne sospirando tra gli alberi, e l'acqua sottostante fu increspata come l'acqua di un recipiente scosso.

E ancora, silenzioso, imponente, inesorabile come il destino, irresistibile come la sorte, quel corpo scuro continuava a muoversi davanti al volto del Sole. Quel cambiamento che tutti avevamo visto descritto cominciò a venire sul cielo. L'azzurro del cielo si fece più scuro, le sue profondità parvero più imperscrutabili che mai, il suo mistero più impenetrabile. Qualcuno disse che era «come una nube temporalesca», ma nessuna nube temporalesca fu mai così profonda, così terribile. Vi era un senso dell'indefinibile, del repellente, che nessuna nube, per quanto cupa, ha mai posseduto.

non era la penombra del crepuscolo quella che vedevo, ma qualcosa di spettrale e pauroso. Gustave Doré avrebbe potuto immaginare una luce simile mentre illustrava l'Inferno di Dante. Allora l'attenzione fu rivolta ai volti della compagnia. Spettrali come il paesaggio. Volti come i volti di uomini morti.

Un altro fenomeno attirò l'attenzione in quel momento. Si osservò che le foglie di un noce americano proiettavano ombre a forma di falce. Una scogliera calcarea lì vicino offriva un bel fondale, e sulla sua superficie ruvida comparivano queste curiose foglie d'ombra. Dappertutto c'era una falce. Dappertutto il Sole registrava, come con un apparecchio autoregistrante, il progresso del processo di oscuramento.

Per tutto questo tempo la falce del Sole era diventata sempre più piccola, e penso che la maggior parte di noi avesse cominciato a pensare che probabilmente non si sarebbe visto molto più di quanto avessimo già testimoniato. Ma proprio allora si vide un debole punto d'argento nel cielo occidentale, a 20 gradi o più dal Sole oscurato. Era Venere. Ma un momento dopo, mentre guardavamo verso le colline occidentali ora cupe, lontano, tetra e terribile, venne ciò che è stato ben chiamato la «Tremenda Ombra». Avanzò come un terrore, o come quell'altra «ombra temuta dall'uomo»—la morte stessa. Un solo sguardo al Sole mostra solo il più sottile bordo di luce. Un solo sguardo in più all'ombra ed essa è già lì.

La gloria dello spettacolo che seguì non spero di descriverla. Avevo pensato che le descrizioni che avevo letto nei giornali e nelle riviste fossero il prodotto congiunto di immaginazione e retorica. Fandonie le avevo giudicate. Ma la gloriosa visione che si spalancò davanti ai nostri occhi era una da non dimenticare mai.

La luce scomparve all'istante. Fu come lo spegnersi di una candela in una stanza buia. E nel preciso momento in cui fu interamente nascosta eruppe la corona. L'ho vista paragonare alla gloria intorno al capo dei santi, ma mai l'aureola dei maestri fu simile alla gloria che eruppe da dietro la Luna. Nel preciso momento dell'oscuramento totale si videro due meteore, e Mercurio, un punto di luce dorata, a sei gradi dal Sole, apparve alla vista. Anche le stelle apparvero a est, segnando con la loro grande luce bianca il posto delle maestose costellazioni. Lontano a nord-ovest fu rivelato un banco di nubi, finora non visto, illuminato da tutta la gloria della luce solare, con i colori rosso, porpora e cremisi che predominavano. L'oscurità è come nessuna oscurità terrestre. È un'oscurità che si può sentire. Un amico cerca di trovare l'ora con un orologio dal quadrante d'oro, e non ci riesce. Un altro tenta di leggere le cifre di un termometro, ma non ci riesce. Ancora una volta guardo indietro al Sole, e poi, visibile senza l'aiuto del telescopio, sul lembo meridionale della Luna, c'è una «protuberanza rossa, come di sangue». Ancora uno sguardo alla Terra. È opaca e spettrale. Ancora uno sguardo alle stelle. Si vedono Arturo, la Lira e Regolo, oltre a Venere e Mercurio. Ancora uno sguardo al Sole. Ci sono i grani di Baily a destra della Luna, una fila di gemme che segna l'arrivo della luce.

E mentre guardiamo viene un lampo, e una luce accecante, abbagliante, travolgente. Non somiglia a nulla se non alla rottura di un grande serbatoio che era stato a lungo sbarrato—luce grata, calda, geniale, benedetta, essa si riversò, dando vita e gioia, salute e pace. Parve una resurrezione. Parve che gli indumenti della tomba fossero stati gettati via, e che la terra si fosse adornata con le vesti di un'eterna giovinezza. L'ombra fuggì davanti all'improvviso scoppio, la vecchia Luna divenne nuova, e ancora una volta ricominciò il suo solenne movimento intorno alla Terra, e con la Terra intorno al Sole.
text.ja:
約三百人の一行は、土曜日の朝7時30分、ヴァイン通りの突き当たりの船着き場をライトル将軍号で出発し、川を下っていった。船は1時15分、市からほぼ百マイル下流のマディソンの船着き場まで進んだ。乗ろうとしていた客を一人置き去りにするだけの間だけ停まって、下りの航行は再開され、船はなおも進み、ウェストポートの二、三マイル上流にあるケンタッキー側の高い断崖がすぐ左手にそびえるところまで来た。そこで巨大な船はもう一度ゆっくりと回頭し、船首は再び帰路へ向けられ、タラップの板が渡された。

一行がどこへ行くかについて全員の考えをまとめたのは、3時20分ごろであった。高さ三百フィートの丘が一行の上に影を落としており、一行のうち何人かは、そんな高さの所は登るものか、史上最高の日食のためであってもだ、と激しく言い張るのに、さほど時間はかからなかった。しかし、気力でも体力でも勝る者たちは、登りの困難に挑んだ。甲板員四、五人をしばらくの間荷役の獣にし、その広い肩に望遠鏡四、五台とクロノメーター一、二台を背負わせて、彼らは登り始めた。

登りは苦しかったが、頂上で得られた眺めは、これほど高い代価を払って買う値打ちがあった。というのも、私は高さ五十フィートの切り立った垂直な断崖の縁に立っており、その麓から地面は川へ向けて急な傾斜で下っていたからである。私はこの丘の額から、二マイル以上先のオハイオ川を越えて、広々と緑のインディアナの低地を見渡し、さらにこの草地を越えて遠く、西の地平線を縁取る遠い丘々まで見渡した。それから北へ向きを変えると、対岸にはなお平らな広がりがあった。もう一度、今度は東へ向きを変えると、四マイル先に川が見え、その波は晴れやかな日の光の中で躍り、きらめいていた。邪魔になるものは数本の木だけで、斧がそれらをたちまち取り除いた。我々の観測の計画に満足しないような人は、よほど気難しい人であったろう。太陽は我々の顔に照りつけ、地平線へ至るその下りの道筋はすべて開けており、その間ずっと、月の塊は、黙って、目に見えず、巨大に、這うのではない、這うというのは忍び寄ることを意味するからだ—進んでいた。

我々の望遠鏡が据え付けられ、大柄で屈強なケンタッキー人が、育ちの悪いトネリコとヒッコリーの茂みを切り払ってしまうころには、もはや一刻の猶予もなかった。大いなる闇の中から、「青く弧を描く天蓋」の中から、古い月が現れ、輝かしい日の光の中にその姿を見せた。一行の一人が叫び声を上げて、この大天文現象の始まりを告げた。それ以後、望遠鏡の据え付けはほとんど終わっていなかったものの、作業は遅々として進んだ。というのも、まばゆい光の巨大な球体をこれほど少しずつ覆っていくヴェールから、どうして目を離していられようか。

他の人々が何を考えていたかは知らない。私の心にまず浮かんだのは神秘の思いであり、次いで畏怖の思いであった。一つの強大な塊が、想像もつかないほど大きなもう一つの塊の前で、堂々たる動きを始めたからである。しかし、その最初の感情が過ぎ去ると、感嘆の思いが浮かんだ。時計を見て、針が4時31分を指しているのに気づいたときのことである。それはまさに、五十年前に、ある天文学者が未来を予見して、今はもう墓の中にいる人々に、月がその時刻に太陽の面の前に立ち、二時間にわたってその光を遮るだろうと告げた時刻であった。しかも、それだけではない。私は、ここから百マイルに満たないところでは部分日食にすぎないこと、そして、その限界が人の畑の境界と同じくらい正確に定められた、幅百四十マイルの狭い帯の中へ、私は皆既日食を見るためにやって来たのだということを思い出した。いや、それ以上である。私は、この皆既日食のまさに中心線のできる限り近くに立っていたのである。

天文学に未来があるなら、過去もある。学ぶべきことがまだ多いとしても、すでに成し遂げられたことも少なくない。私のすぐそばには分光器が立っていた。あの驚くべき器械によって、我々の太陽だけでなく、他の系の太陽も、その構成元素も、私の足もとを流れる水と同じほど正確に知られ、定められる日が、いずれ来るのである。

月が厳かな行進を進めるにつれて、すべての作業は中断された。正確な位置に据わっていない器械は、そのままにされた。一刻一刻が貴重になったからである。我々の一行は科学者の一行ではなく、自分の目を使い、科学の知識は他の源に頼らなければならない。1806年の大日食についてフェニモア・クーパーが記した記述に夢中になっていた人たちでさえ、読むのをやめた。あの美しい記述はいつでも読める。自分自身の目で見られるのは、ただ一度、しかも今だけである。

欠け方が大きくなるにつれて、気温に著しい変化が生じた。我々の多くがこれほど大きな差を予期していたとは思わない。ロバート・ブラウン・ジュニア氏が持っていた寒暖計が日に当てられ、水銀の位置の変化についての情報は、同氏のおかげで得られた。4時50分には89°を示した。4時55分30秒には91°。この点で5時までは動かなかった。その時から次第に下がり始めた。5時5分には88°。5時10分には86°。それ以後は下がり方が速くなり、次の表に示されている。

時刻 ｜ 度 ｜ 時刻 ｜ 度
5:11 ｜ 83.40 ｜ 5:21 ｜ 79.40
5:12 ｜ […] ｜ 5:2[…]½ ｜ 79
5:13 ｜ 84 ｜ 5:23 ｜ 78.30
5:14 ｜ 83.40 ｜ 5:24 ｜ 78
5:15 ｜ 83.30 ｜ 5:25 ｜ 77.20
5:16 ｜ 82.20 ｜ 5:26 ｜ 77
5:17 ｜ 82 ｜ 5:27 ｜ 76.30
5:18 ｜ 81.20 ｜ 5:28 ｜ […]
5:19 ｜ […] ｜ 5:29 ｜ 74.80
5:20 ｜ 80.30 ｜  ｜ 

後の時刻である5時29分に、遮蔽が始まり、2分10秒間続いた。5時31分10秒には、水銀は73°を示した。こうして、1時間足らずのうちに、水銀は18°下がったのである。完全な遮蔽の2分10秒の間には、1度半下がった。

太陽の円盤の約三分の一が隠されたころ、光の変化を見分けられると思った人がいた。光は、それまで気づかれなかった灰色がかった色合いを帯びているように見えた。月が半分まで進んだときには、太陽の三日月形が人々の注意を引き始め、そうなると、光の減少に気づかない者はいなかった。とりわけそれは、水面からの反射に見て取れた。というのも、先ほどまで波は日の光の中できらめいて見る人の目をくらませ、盲目にするほどであったのに対し、今はその上に鈍さがのしかかり、まるで太陽が薄い雲のヴェールを通して照っているかのようであった。また、高い空を飛んでいた巨大なハゲワシ、不吉な鳥が、今は低い層を舞っていることにも気づいた。ちょうどそのとき、風が木々の間をざわざわと吹き抜けてきて、下の水面は、揺すられた器の水のようにさざ波立った。

そして、なおも黙して、厳かに、運命のように容赦なく、宿命のように抗いがたく、あの暗い天体は太陽の面の前を進み続けた。我々が皆、描写されるのを読んだことのある変化が、天に訪れ始めた。空の青は濃さを増し、その深みはこれまで以上に測り知れず、その神秘はいっそう見通しがたく思われた。「雷雲のようだ」と言う者がいたが、これほど深く、これほど恐ろしい雷雲はなかった。名状しがたい、人を寄せつけない感覚があり、どれほど陰鬱な雲であっても、そのようなものを持ったことはない。

私が見たのは黄昏の薄暗さではなく、何か凄惨で恐ろしいものであった。ギュスターヴ・ドレなら、ダンテの『地獄篇』に挿絵を描いていたとき、このような光を思い描いたかもしれない。それから注意は一行の顔に向けられた。風景と同じように凄惨である。死人の顔のような顔であった。

このころ、もう一つの現象が注意を引いた。ヒッコリーの葉が、三日月形の影を落としているのが認められた。近くの石灰岩の断崖がよい背景となり、その粗い表面にこの奇妙な影の葉が映っていた。どこもかしこも三日月であった。どこもかしこも、自動記録の装置のように、暗くなっていく過程の進行を太陽が記録していた。

そのあいだずっと、太陽の三日月はますます小さくなっていた。我々の大半は、これまでに目にしたもの以上のものはおそらく見られないだろうと思い始めていたと思う。だがちょうどそのとき、西の空に、隠れかけた太陽から20度以上離れて、かすかな銀色の点が見えた。金星であった。しかし、その直後、薄暗くなった西の丘のほうを眺めていると、遠くから、陰鬱に、恐ろしく、あの「恐るべき影」と呼ばれてきたものがやって来た。それは恐怖のように、あるいは、もう一つの「人に恐れられる影」、すなわち死そのもののように押し寄せた。太陽を一瞥すれば、ごく細い光の縁が見えるだけである。もう一度影を一瞥すれば、それはもう目の前にある。

それに続いた光景の栄光を、私は描写しようとは思わない。新聞や雑誌で読んだ描写は、想像と修辞の合作だと思っていた。たわごとだと考えていたのである。しかし、我々の目の前に突如現れた輝かしい光景は、決して忘れられないものであった。

光は一瞬で消え去った。暗い部屋で蝋燭を吹き消すようであった。そして太陽がすっかり隠れた瞬間に、コロナが噴き出した。それが聖人たちの頭の周りの栄光にたとえられるのを見たことがあるが、巨匠たちの描いた光輪が、月の背後から噴き出した栄光に似ていたことは一度もない。完全な遮蔽のまさにその瞬間に、流星が二つ見え、太陽から六度離れた金色の光の点である水星が視界に飛び込んだ。東にも星々が現れ、その白く大きな光で、堂々たる星座の位置を示していた。北西のはるか彼方には、それまで見えなかった雲の堤が現れ、日光のあらゆる栄光に照らされて、赤、紫、深紅の色が勝っていた。その闇は地上のいかなる闇とも似ていない。感じ取れるほどの闇である。友人が金色の文字盤の時計で時刻を知ろうとして、できない。別の者が寒暖計の目盛りを読もうとするが、できない。私はもう一度太陽を振り返り、すると、望遠鏡の助けなしに見えるものとして、月の南の縁に「赤い、血のような突起」がある。もう一度地上に目をやる。鈍く、凄惨である。もう一度星々に目をやる。金星と水星のほかに、アルクトゥルス、こと座、レグルスが見える。もう一度太陽に目をやる。月の右側にベイリー・ビーズがあり、光の到来を告げる宝石の列である。

そして、我々が見ているまさにそのとき、閃光が走り、目をくらませ、まばゆく、圧倒する光が来る。それは、長くせき止められていた大きな貯水池が決壊したのにほかならない。ありがたく、暖かく、穏やかで、祝福された光が、奔流となって迸り出て、命と喜び、健康と平和を与えた。それは復活のように思われた。墓の衣が脱ぎ捨てられ、永遠の若さの衣を地球がまとったかのように思われた。突然の迸りの前に影は逃げ去り、古い月は新しい月となって、再び地球の周りを、そして地球とともに太陽の周りを、厳かな動きで進み始めた。

text_orig:
The eclipse of the sun on Saturday last was visible over all the United States and Territories, but a view of the magnificent corona which surrounded the sun was visible only to those who were located on the narrow belt of 156.4 miles in breadth which was swept by the moon's shadow. The light of the sun is so powerful and so overshadowing as to shut out the coronal display to those situated only a few yards outside the limits of totality, though they could discern but the merest thread of sunlight at the moment of greatest obscuration.

For the information of those who were not privileged to witness the phenomenon by reason of location, as well as of those who only saw it with the naked eye within the band of totality, we herewith present a view of the corona, as seen at Des Moines, Iowa, by the writer, through a telescope, sketched by him immediately after the total obscuration had passed, and then submitted to several of the scientific observers present, all of whom recognized it as an accurate portraiture. The cut also shows the rose-colored protuberances, the largest of which were seen by him, but for the positions of the smaller ones, and the exact description of all, he is partially indebted to others, who made them the special subjects of observation, while he directed his attention to the corona, during the 172¾ seconds which intervened between the apparent contacts of the eastern and western edges of the luminaries.

The circular figure on the accompanying diagram represents the moon, her dark side being turned towards the observer. Though her actual diameter is 394 times less than that of the sun, yet she is so much nearer to us that, at the time of the eclipse, her apparent diameter was to that of the sun as 21 to 20, so that the sun was totally obscured during the 2 minutes 52¾ seconds required for her to pass over a space equal to one-twentieth part of the sun's diameter. The apparent motion of her centre was along the line C to D, while the apparent path of the sun's centre may be represented by the line B to A, and the direction of the north and south poles of the heavens by the points marked N and S. The letter Z represents the direction of the zenith; the letters R and L, the direction of right and left. It is evident from the diagram that R was nearly in the direction of northwest; Z, nearly northeast, and L, nearly southeast.

That the light colored rays and the dark rose-colored protuberances (the latter represented by black spots on the diagram) belonged to the sun, and not to the moon, is evident from the fact that when the edges of the sun and moon coincided at D, at the first instant of total obscuration, the moon's edge lapping some distance over the sun at C, the protuberances on the upper left side were visible, and the corona on that side was larger, while, when the moon had advanced so that the edges nearly connected at C, and the moon lapped over at D, the protuberances on the D side were invisible, while those on the C side came into view, and the corona on the latter side was largest. Accepting this view we obtain a gauge of dimension which enables us to approximately measure the dimensions of the several parts of the corona and the protuberances.

Thus: the sun is known to subtend an actual diameter of 851,736 miles, while his apparent angular diameter at the time of eclipse was 31 minutes, 37.6 seconds of space, corresponding to 412.76 miles to each second, or very nearly 71,000 miles (70,979.66) to each digit, or twelfth part of the sun's diameter. But in order to find the total amount of projection, it is evident that we must take into account not only the amount of protrusion beyond the edge of the moon, but also the amount due to the overlapping of the moon's edge at the point and instant of observation.

THE CORONA.

The corona was remarkably different from all preconceived notions on the subject, and from all previous descriptions, both in size and shape. It has always been represented as nearly annular (ring formed), of about equal breadth all the way round the edge of the moon, and not more than one-tenth of her apparent diameter. The corona of Saturday last was exceedingly irregular in its outline, and in some places projected to a distance fully half that of the apparent diameter of the moon, or nearly 500,000 miles. Our diagram shows the relative lengths of the several portions, except that on the sides the length is slightly constricted by the width of the column rules.

The greatest length was almost identical with the direction of the moon's path, across the face of the sun, which very nearly coincided with the plane of the ecliptic. From the east side (direction from D) a mass of light shot out to the distance of five or six digits; it was about thirty degrees wide at the base, and shaped nearly like the remote half of a silver poplar leaf. Near the moon it shone with an almost uniform white light, but within a short space it broke up into brilliant rays, almost parallel with each other, and all pointing nearly towards the centre of the diagram. Still farther out these rays assumed more of a streaky character, seeming to lie against a darker background, and towards the summit they faded away into a more diffused and milder light, though still distinct and bright. Near the extremity it appeared more like a cumulus cloud, but the central direction of the rays was plainly visible. It melted away into the azure background almost imperceptibly, but the outline was perfect, except at the very extremity of the leaf shaped mass. On the other side of the disc (direction from A, C) was a corresponding tongue, but less regular, and extending only about two-thirds as far into the void. This portion was more brilliant near the base than its counterpart, and was sharply defined at the very extremity, the rays blending so thickly that it required a steady gaze to separate them. The extent of this portion was about 255,000 miles. Professor Lane saw the light reflected from the moon's edge at the distance of 54,000 miles from the sun's body, while the light was reflected from the other edge at a distance of 74,000 miles. We compute the total width of the corona in the direction through A D, including the sun's body, at 1,600,000 miles.

The broadest mass of coronal light was visible on the left (in the south-east quarter). This sprang from an arc of about 50 degrees on the moon's circumference, to a height of three digits, or 224,000 miles. This mass was more diffused than either of the others, and separated near the extremity into narrow leaflets of light, something like the flame from a thinly spread bed of coals, only there was no red, the light being pure white, with a faint coruscation. Opposite to this, on the right, was another leaf-spread mass of four digits in height, on a base of 20 to 25 degrees, and like a parabola in the general outline, which was, however, broken up on the outer side into jets. Another broad sheet sprang up on the north-east (toward the zenith) nearly rectangular in shape, and three to four digits high, the upper third part being divided irregularly into tongues of light, formed by assemblages of rays. Between these larger masses the circumference of the lunar orb was filled up by radiate lines of brilliant light, extending on an average a digit and a half in height, or 125,000 miles from the sun's surface. It was noticeable that this continuous band was the most narrow on the lower left hand side (southwest by south) averaging about two-thirds of the width elsewhere, and was badly broken on its entire outline, as if the regularity were interfered with by the action of the string of bead-like protuberances jutting up through the interior portion of its volume.

The full amount of this irregularity was not perceptible with the naked eye, but the general distribution of long and short rays was the same. To the unaided vision the narrower portions of the corona were visible and bright; but the tongue-like extensions faded out into nothingness, whereas the telescope gave a definite outline all around, except at the summit of the first-named protrusion. We do not claim that the relative lengths of the different portions were exactly as laid down here; they were estimated at the instant, and transferred to paper directly; but the time allowed for observation (less than three minutes) was so short that it can scarcely be considered possible to reproduce every part of the outline with unfailing accuracy.

As stated in the letters from Des Moines, the images of the corona taken in the camera by Dr. Curtis, of the United States Navy, do not show so great a breadth of outline as is here represented, probably for the reason that the light of the outer portions was too faint, by comparison, to fix an image on the plate, while the more brilliant portions were burning their impress on the apparatus. The photographs show the corona to be least broad in the region of the protuberances, and have preserved the impress of as much of its breadth as corresponds to a distance of 105,000 miles from the sun's body, whence we may conclude that the photosphere extends to at least that distance, while the observations of Prof. Lane show that at three-fourths of that distance it possesses enough of illuminating power to light up the moon's surface to an extent sufficient to cause a reflection of its rays through a distance of 225,000 miles.

A legitimate conclusion from this, and through spectroscopic observations detailed in our reports, is that the solid body of the sun is surrounded by a self-luminous atmosphere of at least one hundred thousand miles in thickness, or one-fourth part of his radius, this giving the image fixed in the camera, and that outside of the light (photosphere is a non-luminous envelope or atmosphere, shining to us by means of the light received from the interior shell, which it reflects to our eyes. This non-luminous envelope or atmosphere, must be at least 600,000 miles in thickness, and perhaps twice that amount, as its density must decrease with the distance till it loses its reflective power. It is not impossible that the prolongation in the direction C A B, gives rise to the phenomenon known as the Zodiacal light; and rises sufficiently near the orbit of Mercury to cause the disturbances in his movements which have been ascribed to a mythical belt of planetoids.

These are represented on the diagram in black; their apparent color was a pink red. The instant that the last thin film of light, with its middle at D, had vanished, leaving the sun in utter darkness, and simultaneously with the outflash of the corona, the line of protuberances extending from P to B also burst upon the view. The one at the lowest point was the largest. All saw the upper portion, which occupied about 16 degrees on the moon's disc, and projected 56,000 miles from the sun's edge, or fully one-half the average height of the photosphere. Dr. Hilgard saw and described the lower, or pendant portion, which was estimated to be 100,000 miles long, by 20,000 miles wide, making a total protrusion of 156,000 miles. The protuberance at L, and the one immediately below it, were also visible to the naked eye; they were rectangular, and were estimated at 20,000 miles high, with bases of five and eight degrees on the circumference. The photograph showed the three more fancifully-shaped ones near the eastern quarter, which were also more faint in outline, seeming as if one part lay far behind the other, which crosses it in the diagram. Hence the cross-shaped figure at B was probably made up of two independent protuberances, the horizontal portion lying several hundred miles farther from the eye of the spectator than the part which seemed to stand nearly upright. In the lower-left quarter a string of bead-like protuberances were also visible with the aid of the telescope. Their comparative size is necessarily exaggerated on our diagram; they were, perhaps, not more than 5,000 miles high, and dropped out of sight in rapid succession in a few seconds, as the moon advanced rapidly in the direction C to D. And now the three larger ones at D, B grew smaller, fading from the view about the middle of totality, which fact showed them to have an altitude of about 25,000 miles.

At this time the western edge of the moon had advanced sufficiently in its course to uncover the protuberances on that side, and the three shown from A to R flashed on the vision, only the exterior portions being visible at first, but soon growing out farther and farther till the three exhibited an altitude of at least 20,000 miles, by an aggregate breadth of fully 20 degrees on the base. Meanwhile the protuberance at P grew larger, unsteadily, as the moon's edge at that point neared the edge of the sun, but it then seemed to decrease shortly before the total phase ended, showing an actual change in volume, though the character of the outlines did not perceptibly vary. These four were distinctly visible till the last instant, when they vanished with the corona, as a star disappears from the view when a flash of lightning illumines the firmament.

The spectroscope had already told us that these protuberances are masses of incandescent matter, and some of its constituent elements have been determined to be identical with substances peculiar to us, as iron, sodium, magnesium and hydrogen. But it was reserved to Professor Harkness to discover that there is a constant decrease in the number of elements in proportion to the height above the sun's surface. Thus the summit contains no element but hydrogen, and sodium appears a little lower, while iron is, possibly, the element to rise with the greatest difficulty, and to fall back soonest into the bosom of the sun. We have also reason to believe that these protuberances are identical with the dark masses known as "spots" when seen on that part of the sun's atmosphere which is between us and his body.

So much, then, we know of the constitution of the sun that he is surrounded by a double atmosphere, and that the interior one is self-luminous and the scene of violent changes connected with the formation and movement of immense bulks of incandescent matter. We know, further, that many of the substances which are found in large quantities on the earth exist also in the sun, and we may reason from analogy that other yet undiscovered terrene elements join these to make up the grand total of solar matter. But beyond this lies a vast void belonging to the regions of the unknown; probably much that will forever remain "unknowable" by mortals. But where knowledge ends speculation begins.

It has been thought that the lumin-luminous and non-luminous atmospheres of the sun are like two air strata in our atmosphere; not absolutely separable, nor divided by a line the position of which can be indicated. This is, we believe, the general theory with those who entertain one, that it is but a general distinction, like the discrimination between upper and lower portions of our atmosphere, the one merging into the other by imperceptible gradations, and the self-luminosity ceasing only when the density becomes too small to admit of that intensity of vibration which is supposed necessary to originate the sensation of light.

This may be so, but it seems quite as probable that the sun's condition is similar, in respect to form, with that of the earth before the continents were upheaved by volcanic force. Then the ocean covered the land, and was itself surrounded by an outer atmosphere of air, the two oceans, then as now, not only balancing each other, but being mutually necessary to the integrity of character pertaining to each. Of course it is not necessary that the photosphere should be composed of anything like what we call water, and indeed we have no particular reason to believe that oxygen, the chief constituent of water, is present at all. But it is necessarily a somewhat dense fluid, and is probably in a state of more intense motion than any intermovement of particles of which we have any knowledge. There is no doubt that this fluid is also intensely hot, but that is probably not a result of c[…]ustion, and is more a consequence of its rapid motion than a necessary condition of heat in the solar rays. So far as we know, light and heat are phenomenal only—mere conditions, not material entities—and these sensations are communicated only by the intermediate vibrations of material particles. It is always cold on the tops of high mountains, though there be level enough to admit of a large amount of earth radiation, and we must conclude that the difference is principally due to a lessened density of the atmosphere, which presents fewer particles to be vibrated in the passage of the solar rays; hence less of motion; hence less of the sensation of heat. The sun's rays are warm and light to us only because they vibrate through certain media. Take away those media, and the sensation is absent.

We have every reason to believe that the earth and moon have existed under somewhat similar conditions to those now witnessed in the sun, with this probable difference that the earth has a comparative excess of oxygen, and the sun of hydrogen, while the moon is deficient in both of those elements. To this difference we may perhaps look for consolation against the fear that the sun will be burned out ultimately, and leave our posterity a thousand generations hence to die out of cold. The above view is perfectly consistent, too, with the idea that the sun may be a fit residence for animated beings, organized in adaptation to the situation, and enables us to drop the difficulty which meets us in the attempt to conceive of an eternally self-sustaining conflagration.

text.zh-Hans:
上星期六之日食，合众国及各领地皆可见，然环日之壮丽日冕，唯处于月影所扫过之狭带者得见，此带宽一百五十六点四英里。日光至强，其辉遮蔽一切，致位于全食界外仅数码之人，亦不得见日冕之景，虽于食甚之刻，亦仅能辨极细之一线日光。

兹为因所在之地而未能亲见此象者，及仅于全食带内以肉眼观之者，特附日冕一图，乃本文作者于艾奥瓦州得梅因以望远镜所见，于全食甫过即草绘，复呈在场数位科学观测者过目，诸人皆认为所绘确切。图中并绘玫瑰色突出物，其最大者为作者亲见，至较小者之位置及诸突出物之确切描述，则部分借助他人，彼等专以此为观测对象，而作者则于日月东西两缘视接触之间所隔一百七十二又四分之三秒内，专注日冕。

附图中圆形者代表月，其暗面向观者。月之实径虽较日小三百九十四倍，然距我辈近得多，故食时其视径与日视径之比为二十一比二十，是以日被全掩历二分五十二又四分之三秒，此即月越过相当于日径二十分之一之空间所需之时。月心视行沿 C 至 D 之线，日心之视路可以 B 至 A 之线表示，天之南北极方向以所标 N、S 二点表示。Z 示天顶之方向，R 与 L 示右与左之方向。由图可明，R 约在西北，Z 约在东北，L 约在东南。

色浅之光线与色暗之玫瑰色突出物（后者于图中以黑点示之）属日而不属月，其证甚明：全食初起一刹那，日月之缘于 D 处相合，月缘于 C 处覆于日上若干距离，其时左上方之突出物可见，该侧日冕亦较大；及月前行，二缘于 C 处几相连而月于 D 处覆日，则 D 侧突出物不可见，C 侧者则入目，而此侧日冕最大。既取此说，即得一度量之准，可借以约略量度日冕诸部及突出物之大小。

如是：已知日之实径为八十五万一千七百三十六英里，而食时其视角径为三十一角分三十七点六角秒，每一角秒合四百一十二点七六英里，亦即每指，或曰日径十二分之一，几七万一千英里（七万零九百七十九点六六）。然欲求突出之总量，显须不仅计其出月缘之外者，并须计观测之点与刻月缘所覆之量。

日冕

日冕于大小与形状，皆与世人先入之见及以往一切描述大异。向来所绘，几成环形（圆环状），绕月缘各处宽度大略相等，不逾月视径十分之一。上星期六之日冕，轮廓极不规则，若干处伸出之距，足月视径之半，几近五十万英里。附图示诸部相对长度，惟两侧之长因栏线之宽稍受压缩。

最长者与月越日面之路径方向几全相合，此路径又几与黄道面相合。自东侧（自 D 起之方向）一团光射出，远五六指；基部宽约三十度，形几如银白杨叶之远半。近月处其光白而几匀，然未远即裂为明亮光线，彼此几平行，皆约指向图心。更远处，此诸光线益呈条纹状，似倚于较暗之背景，近顶端则渐隐为更弥散柔和之光，然仍清晰而亮。近末端处较似积云，而光线之中央走向犹明晰可见。其消融于蔚蓝背景几不可察，然轮廓完整，唯叶形光团之最末端除外。日盘另一侧（自 A、C 起之方向）有一相对之舌，然较不规则，伸入空际仅及前者三分之二。此部近基处较其对应者更明亮，而于最末端界线分明，光线交融甚密，须凝视方能分辨。此部之长约二十五万五千英里。Lane 教授见月缘所反射之光，距日体五万四千英里，而另一缘所反射之光，距七万四千英里。吾侪计日冕沿 A D 方向之总宽，连日体在内，为一百六十万英里。

日冕光最宽之一团见于左方（东南象限）。其起自月周约五十度之弧，高三指，合二十二万四千英里。此团较他二团更弥散，近末端分为窄细光叶，略如薄铺炭床之焰，唯无红色，光纯白，微有闪烁。与之相对，右方另有一叶状展开之团，高四指，基部二十至二十五度，大致轮廓如抛物线，然外侧裂为数股喷射。又一宽幅自东北（向天顶）升起，形几成矩，高三至四指，其上三分之一不规则分为数舌，由光线之簇聚而成。此诸大团之间，月轮周缘为辉煌放射线所填，平均高一指半，即距日面十二万五千英里。可注意者，此连续之带在左下侧（西南偏南）最窄，平均约为他处三分之二，且整个轮廓残缺不整，似为一串念珠状突出物穿出其体积内部之作用所扰，致失其规则。

此不规则之全貌，肉眼不能尽见，然长短光线之大致分布则同。就未借助之目力，日冕较窄处可见而明亮，而舌状延伸则消失于无形，望远镜则四周轮廓皆明确，唯首述突出之顶端除外。吾侪不敢谓诸部相对长度确如此处所绘；其乃当时目估，直接移之于纸，惟所许观测之时（不及三分钟）甚短，实难谓轮廓每一部皆能一一无误重现。

如得梅因来函所言，美国海军 Curtis 博士以暗箱所摄日冕之像，其轮廓之宽不及此处所绘，或因外部之光较之过于微弱，不足在板上留影，而较明亮部分正将其印痕烧入器械。照片显示日冕在突出物之区域最窄，所留印痕之宽相当于距日体十万零五千英里，由是可断光球至少延及此距，而 Lane 教授之观测示，于此距离四分之三处，其照明力足以照亮月面，致其光线反射达二十二万五千英里。

由此及本报所详述之分光镜观测，可得一合理结论：日之固体为自发光之大气所环绕，厚至少十万英里，即其半径之四分之一，此即摄于暗箱之像所示，而发光光球之外，有一不发光之外壳或大气，其光之达于吾人，乃凭反射自内层所受之光。此不发光之壳或大气，厚必至少六十万英里，或更加倍，因其密度必随距离而减，至失其反射之力方止。沿 C A B 方向之延伸，未必不即生所谓黄道光之象，且升至颇近水星轨道，以致扰其运动，此扰动向来归诸虚构之小行星带。

此等突出物于图中以黑色绘出，其视色粉红。中心在 D 之最后一缕薄光消去，日遂陷于全黑，同时日冕迸发，自 P 至 B 之一线突出物亦骤然呈现。位于最低点者最大。众皆见其上部，占月面约十六度，突出日缘五万六千英里，足光球平均高度之半。Hilgard 博士见而述其下部，即下垂之部，估长十万英里，宽二万英里，合计突出十五万六千英里。L 处之突出物及其紧下者，肉眼亦可见；皆矩形，估高二万英里，基部在圆周上占五度与八度。照片显示近东象限有形状较奇之三者，轮廓亦较淡，似一部远在他部之后，而他部于图中交叉于其上。故 B 处十字形，或由二独立突出物合成，横部距观者之目较似近乎直立之部远数百英里。左下象限亦有一串念珠状突出物，借望远镜可见。其相对大小于附图中必有夸大；彼等或不过高五千英里，月沿 C 至 D 之方向速进，数秒内先后相继没入不见。至于 D、B 之三较大者，渐小，约于全食中段隐去，是知其高约二万五千英里。

此时月之西缘已行进足以露出该侧突出物，自 A 至 R 所示三者倏现于目，初仅外部可见，旋愈长愈远，至三者之高至少二万英里，基部合计宽整二十度。其间 P 处突出物渐大，不稳，因该处月缘近日缘，然于全食将终前不久似又减小，显实有体积之变，而轮廓性质未觉有异。此四者至最后一刹那皆明晰可见，与日冕同没，如闪电照亮天宇时一星自视中消失。

分光镜已告吾侪，此诸突出物乃白热之物质团，其若干成分已定与地上所独有之物同，如铁、钠、镁及氢。然发现元素数目随日面以上高度而恒减者，则留待 Harkness 教授。故其顶只含氢，钠稍低而现，铁则或为最难上升而最先坠回日怀者。吾侪亦有理由信此诸突出物与所谓「黑子」之暗团同，当其见于日之大气介于吾人与日体之间之部分时。

于日之构成，吾侪所知者止此：其周有双层大气，内层自发光，且为庞大白热物质团形成与运动相关之剧变之场。又知地上大量所有诸物，多亦存于日中，类比而推，其他尚未发现之地上元素亦与此并列，以成日质之总数。然此外有一片浩渺空白，属未知之域；其中大半，将永为凡人所「不可知」。然知识尽处，臆测由此而起。

有人以为，日之发光与不发光二大气，如吾人大气中之二气层；不能绝对分离，亦无可指明其位之界线。吾侪信，持此说者大抵皆以为，此仅概略之分，如吾人大气上下二部之别，一渐入于他，其渐不可察，而自发光唯止于密度过小、不足容被认为生光感所必需之强度振动之处。

或然，然日之情形，就形态言，与大陆未为火山之力隆起前之地球相似，似亦同样可能。其时海洋覆陆，海洋自身又为外层大气所环，二洋彼时如今，不独互相平衡，且为各自品格之完整所相互必需。当然，光球不必由近乎吾人所谓水者构成，实亦无特别理由信水之主要成分氧存在其中。然其必为稍浓之流体，且或处于较吾人所知任何粒子相互运动更剧烈之运动状态。此流体亦极热，无可疑，然此热或非由[…]而生，而更多为其迅速运动之结果，非日光中热之必要条件。就吾侪所知，光与热仅为现象——纯属状态，非物质实体——此等感觉唯由物质粒子之中介振动传递。高山之巅恒寒，虽有平坦之地足容大量地面辐射，吾侪必断其差异主要由大气密度减小所致，日光线穿过时所遇可振动之粒子较少，故运动较少，故热感较少。日光之于吾人，温且明，只因其经某些介质而振动；去其介质，则其感觉无从有。

吾侪有充分理由信地球与月曾处于与今日之日所见者颇相类之状态，所可能异者，地球氧相对过剩，日则氢过剩，而月二者皆乏。或可由此异得慰，以免日终将烧尽、致千代之后吾侪后嗣冻绝之忧。上述之见，亦与日或为有生之物之适居相合，彼等之构造适其处境，且使吾侪得免设想永自维持之大火时所遇之难。
text.zh-Hant:
上星期六之日食，合眾國及各領地皆可見，然環日之壯麗日冕，唯處於月影所掃過之狹帶者得見，此帶寬一百五十六點四英里。日光至強，其輝遮蔽一切，致位於全食界外僅數碼之人，亦不得見日冕之景，雖於食甚之刻，亦僅能辨極細之一線日光。

茲為因所在之地而未能親見此象者，及僅於全食帶內以肉眼觀之者，特附日冕一圖，乃本文作者於艾奧瓦州得梅因以望遠鏡所見，於全食甫過即草繪，覆呈在場數位科學觀測者過目，諸人皆認為所繪確切。圖中並繪玫瑰色突出物，其最大者為作者親見，至較小者之位置及諸突出物之確切描述，則部分藉助他人，彼等專以此為觀測對象，而作者則於日月東西兩緣視接觸之間所隔一百七十二又四分之三秒內，專注日冕。

附圖中圓形者代表月，其暗面向觀者。月之實徑雖較日小三百九十四倍，然距我輩近得多，故食時其視徑與日視徑之比為二十一比二十，是以日被全掩歷二分五十二又四分之三秒，此即月越過相當於日徑二十分之一之空間所需之時。月心視行沿 C 至 D 之線，日心之視路可以 B 至 A 之線表示，天之南北極方向以所標 N、S 二點表示。Z 示天頂之方向，R 與 L 示右與左之方向。由圖可明，R 約在西北，Z 約在東北，L 約在東南。

色淺之光線與色暗之玫瑰色突出物（後者於圖中以黑點示之）屬日而不屬月，其證甚明：全食初起一剎那，日月之緣於 D 處相合，月緣於 C 處覆於日上若干距離，其時左上方之突出物可見，該側日冕亦較大；及月前行，二緣於 C 處幾相連而月於 D 處覆日，則 D 側突出物不可見，C 側者則入目，而此側日冕最大。既取此説，即得一度量之準，可藉以約略量度日冕諸部及突出物之大小。

如是：已知日之實徑為八十五萬一千七百三十六英里，而食時其視角徑為三十一角分三十七點六角秒，每一角秒合四百一十二點七六英里，亦即每指，或曰日徑十二分之一，幾七萬一千英里（七萬零九百七十九點六六）。然欲求突出之總量，顯須不僅計其出月緣之外者，並須計觀測之點與刻月緣所覆之量。

日冕

日冕於大小與形狀，皆與世人先入之見及以往一切描述大異。向來所繪，幾成環形（圓環狀），繞月緣各處寬度大略相等，不逾月視徑十分之一。上星期六之日冕，輪廓極不規則，若干處伸出之距，足月視徑之半，幾近五十萬英里。附圖示諸部相對長度，惟兩側之長因欄線之寬稍受壓縮。

最長者與月越日面之路徑方向幾全相合，此路徑又幾與黃道面相合。自東側（自 D 起之方向）一團光射出，遠五六指；基部寬約三十度，形幾如銀白楊葉之遠半。近月處其光白而幾勻，然未遠即裂為明亮光線，彼此幾平行，皆約指向圖心。更遠處，此諸光線益呈條紋狀，似倚於較暗之背景，近頂端則漸隱為更彌散柔和之光，然仍清晰而亮。近末端處較似積雲，而光線之中央走向猶明晰可見。其消融於蔚藍背景幾不可察，然輪廓完整，唯葉形光團之最末端除外。日盤另一側（自 A、C 起之方向）有一相對之舌，然較不規則，伸入空際僅及前者三分之二。此部近基處較其對應者更明亮，而於最末端界線分明，光線交融甚密，須凝視方能分辨。此部之長約二十五萬五千英里。Lane 教授見月緣所反射之光，距日體五萬四千英里，而另一緣所反射之光，距七萬四千英里。吾儕計日冕沿 A D 方向之總寬，連日體在內，為一百六十萬英里。

日冕光最寬之一團見於左方（東南象限）。其起自月周約五十度之弧，高三指，合二十二萬四千英里。此團較他二團更彌散，近末端分為窄細光葉，略如薄鋪炭牀之焰，唯無紅色，光純白，微有閃爍。與之相對，右方另有一葉狀展開之團，高四指，基部二十至二十五度，大致輪廓如拋物線，然外側裂為數股噴射。又一寬幅自東北（向天頂）升起，形幾成矩，高三至四指，其上三分之一不規則分為數舌，由光線之簇聚而成。此諸大團之間，月輪周緣為輝煌放射線所填，平均高一指半，即距日面十二萬五千英里。可注意者，此連續之帶在左下側（西南偏南）最窄，平均約為他處三分之二，且整個輪廓殘缺不整，似為一串念珠狀突出物穿出其體積內部之作用所擾，致失其規則。

此不規則之全貌，肉眼不能盡見，然長短光線之大致分佈則同。就未藉助之目力，日冕較窄處可見而明亮，而舌狀延伸則消失於無形，望遠鏡則四周輪廓皆明確，唯首述突出之頂端除外。吾儕不敢謂諸部相對長度確如此處所繪；其乃當時目估，直接移之於紙，惟所許觀測之時（不及三分鐘）甚短，實難謂輪廓每一部皆能一一無誤重現。

如得梅因來函所言，美國海軍 Curtis 博士以暗箱所攝日冕之像，其輪廓之寬不及此處所繪，或因外部之光較之過於微弱，不足在板上留影，而較明亮部分正將其印痕燒入器械。照片顯示日冕在突出物之區域最窄，所留印痕之寬相當於距日體十萬零五千英里，由是可斷光球至少延及此距，而 Lane 教授之觀測示，於此距離四分之三處，其照明力足以照亮月面，致其光線反射達二十二萬五千英里。

由此及本報所詳述之分光鏡觀測，可得一合理結論：日之固體為自發光之大氣所環繞，厚至少十萬英里，即其半徑之四分之一，此即攝於暗箱之像所示，而發光光球之外，有一不發光之外殼或大氣，其光之達於吾人，乃憑反射自內層所受之光。此不發光之殼或大氣，厚必至少六十萬英里，或更加倍，因其密度必隨距離而減，至失其反射之力方止。沿 C A B 方向之延伸，未必不即生所謂黃道光之象，且升至頗近水星軌道，以致擾其運動，此擾動向來歸諸虛構之小行星帶。

此等突出物於圖中以黑色繪出，其視色粉紅。中心在 D 之最後一縷薄光消去，日遂陷於全黑，同時日冕迸發，自 P 至 B 之一線突出物亦驟然呈現。位於最低點者最大。眾皆見其上部，占月面約十六度，突出日緣五萬六千英里，足光球平均高度之半。Hilgard 博士見而述其下部，即下垂之部，估長十萬英里，寬二萬英里，合計突出十五萬六千英里。L 處之突出物及其緊下者，肉眼亦可見；皆矩形，估高二萬英里，基部在圓周上占五度與八度。照片顯示近東象限有形狀較奇之三者，輪廓亦較淡，似一部遠在他部之後，而他部於圖中交叉於其上。故 B 處十字形，或由二獨立突出物合成，橫部距觀者之目較似近乎直立之部遠數百英里。左下象限亦有一串念珠狀突出物，借望遠鏡可見。其相對大小於附圖中必有誇大；彼等或不過高五千英里，月沿 C 至 D 之方向速進，數秒內先後相繼沒入不見。至於 D、B 之三較大者，漸小，約於全食中段隱去，是知其高約二萬五千英里。

此時月之西緣已行進足以露出該側突出物，自 A 至 R 所示三者倏現於目，初僅外部可見，旋愈長愈遠，至三者之高至少二萬英里，基部合計寬整二十度。其間 P 處突出物漸大，不穩，因該處月緣近日緣，然於全食將終前不久似又減小，顯實有體積之變，而輪廓性質未覺有異。此四者至最後一剎那皆明晰可見，與日冕同沒，如閃電照亮天宇時一星自視中消失。

分光鏡已告吾儕，此諸突出物乃白熱之物質團，其若干成分已定與地上所獨有之物同，如鐵、鈉、鎂及氫。然發現元素數目隨日面以上高度而恆減者，則留待 Harkness 教授。故其頂只含氫，鈉稍低而現，鐵則或為最難上升而最先墜回日懷者。吾儕亦有理由信此諸突出物與所謂「黑子」之暗團同，當其見於日之大氣介於吾人與日體之間之部分時。

於日之構成，吾儕所知者止此：其周有雙層大氣，內層自發光，且為龐大白熱物質團形成與運動相關之劇變之場。又知地上大量所有諸物，多亦存於日中，類比而推，其他尚未發現之地上元素亦與此並列，以成日質之總數。然此外有一片浩渺空白，屬未知之域；其中大半，將永為凡人所「不可知」。然知識盡處，臆測由此而起。

有人以為，日之發光與不發光二大氣，如吾人大氣中之二氣層；不能絕對分離，亦無可指明其位之界線。吾儕信，持此説者大抵皆以為，此僅概略之分，如吾人大氣上下二部之別，一漸入於他，其漸不可察，而自發光唯止於密度過小、不足容被認為生光感所必需之強度振動之處。

或然，然日之情形，就形態言，與大陸未為火山之力隆起前之地球相似，似亦同樣可能。其時海洋覆陸，海洋自身又為外層大氣所環，二洋彼時如今，不獨互相平衡，且為各自品格之完整所相互必需。當然，光球不必由近乎吾人所謂水者構成，實亦無特別理由信水之主要成分氧存在其中。然其必為稍濃之流體，且或處於較吾人所知任何粒子相互運動更劇烈之運動狀態。此流體亦極熱，無可疑，然此熱或非由[…]而生，而更多為其迅速運動之結果，非日光中熱之必要條件。就吾儕所知，光與熱僅為現象——純屬狀態，非物質實體——此等感覺唯由物質粒子之中介振動傳遞。高山之巔恆寒，雖有平坦之地足容大量地面輻射，吾儕必斷其差異主要由大氣密度減小所致，日光線穿過時所遇可振動之粒子較少，故運動較少，故熱感較少。日光之於吾人，温且明，只因其經某些介質而振動；去其介質，則其感覺無從有。

吾儕有充分理由信地球與月曾處於與今日之日所見者頗相類之狀態，所可能異者，地球氧相對過剩，日則氫過剩，而月二者皆乏。或可由此異得慰，以免日終將燒盡、致千代之後吾儕後嗣凍絕之憂。上述之見，亦與日或為有生之物之適居相合，彼等之構造適其處境，且使吾儕得免設想永自維持之大火時所遇之難。
text.en:
The eclipse of the sun on Saturday last was visible over all the United States and Territories, but a view of the magnificent corona which surrounded the sun was visible only to those who were located on the narrow belt of 156.4 miles in breadth which was swept by the moon's shadow. The light of the sun is so powerful and so overshadowing as to shut out the coronal display to those situated only a few yards outside the limits of totality, though they could discern but the merest thread of sunlight at the moment of greatest obscuration.

For the information of those who were not privileged to witness the phenomenon by reason of location, as well as of those who only saw it with the naked eye within the band of totality, we herewith present a view of the corona, as seen at Des Moines, Iowa, by the writer, through a telescope, sketched by him immediately after the total obscuration had passed, and then submitted to several of the scientific observers present, all of whom recognized it as an accurate portraiture. The cut also shows the rose-colored protuberances, the largest of which were seen by him, but for the positions of the smaller ones, and the exact description of all, he is partially indebted to others, who made them the special subjects of observation, while he directed his attention to the corona, during the 172¾ seconds which intervened between the apparent contacts of the eastern and western edges of the luminaries.

The circular figure on the accompanying diagram represents the moon, her dark side being turned towards the observer. Though her actual diameter is 394 times less than that of the sun, yet she is so much nearer to us that, at the time of the eclipse, her apparent diameter was to that of the sun as 21 to 20, so that the sun was totally obscured during the 2 minutes 52¾ seconds required for her to pass over a space equal to one-twentieth part of the sun's diameter. The apparent motion of her centre was along the line C to D, while the apparent path of the sun's centre may be represented by the line B to A, and the direction of the north and south poles of the heavens by the points marked N and S. The letter Z represents the direction of the zenith; the letters R and L, the direction of right and left. It is evident from the diagram that R was nearly in the direction of northwest; Z, nearly northeast, and L, nearly southeast.

That the light colored rays and the dark rose-colored protuberances (the latter represented by black spots on the diagram) belonged to the sun, and not to the moon, is evident from the fact that when the edges of the sun and moon coincided at D, at the first instant of total obscuration, the moon's edge lapping some distance over the sun at C, the protuberances on the upper left side were visible, and the corona on that side was larger, while, when the moon had advanced so that the edges nearly connected at C, and the moon lapped over at D, the protuberances on the D side were invisible, while those on the C side came into view, and the corona on the latter side was largest. Accepting this view we obtain a gauge of dimension which enables us to approximately measure the dimensions of the several parts of the corona and the protuberances.

Thus: the sun is known to subtend an actual diameter of 851,736 miles, while his apparent angular diameter at the time of eclipse was 31 minutes, 37.6 seconds of space, corresponding to 412.76 miles to each second, or very nearly 71,000 miles (70,979.66) to each digit, or twelfth part of the sun's diameter. But in order to find the total amount of projection, it is evident that we must take into account not only the amount of protrusion beyond the edge of the moon, but also the amount due to the overlapping of the moon's edge at the point and instant of observation.

THE CORONA.

The corona was remarkably different from all preconceived notions on the subject, and from all previous descriptions, both in size and shape. It has always been represented as nearly annular (ring formed), of about equal breadth all the way round the edge of the moon, and not more than one-tenth of her apparent diameter. The corona of Saturday last was exceedingly irregular in its outline, and in some places projected to a distance fully half that of the apparent diameter of the moon, or nearly 500,000 miles. Our diagram shows the relative lengths of the several portions, except that on the sides the length is slightly constricted by the width of the column rules.

The greatest length was almost identical with the direction of the moon's path, across the face of the sun, which very nearly coincided with the plane of the ecliptic. From the east side (direction from D) a mass of light shot out to the distance of five or six digits; it was about thirty degrees wide at the base, and shaped nearly like the remote half of a silver poplar leaf. Near the moon it shone with an almost uniform white light, but within a short space it broke up into brilliant rays, almost parallel with each other, and all pointing nearly towards the centre of the diagram. Still farther out these rays assumed more of a streaky character, seeming to lie against a darker background, and towards the summit they faded away into a more diffused and milder light, though still distinct and bright. Near the extremity it appeared more like a cumulus cloud, but the central direction of the rays was plainly visible. It melted away into the azure background almost imperceptibly, but the outline was perfect, except at the very extremity of the leaf shaped mass. On the other side of the disc (direction from A, C) was a corresponding tongue, but less regular, and extending only about two-thirds as far into the void. This portion was more brilliant near the base than its counterpart, and was sharply defined at the very extremity, the rays blending so thickly that it required a steady gaze to separate them. The extent of this portion was about 255,000 miles. Professor Lane saw the light reflected from the moon's edge at the distance of 54,000 miles from the sun's body, while the light was reflected from the other edge at a distance of 74,000 miles. We compute the total width of the corona in the direction through A D, including the sun's body, at 1,600,000 miles.

The broadest mass of coronal light was visible on the left (in the south-east quarter). This sprang from an arc of about 50 degrees on the moon's circumference, to a height of three digits, or 224,000 miles. This mass was more diffused than either of the others, and separated near the extremity into narrow leaflets of light, something like the flame from a thinly spread bed of coals, only there was no red, the light being pure white, with a faint coruscation. Opposite to this, on the right, was another leaf-spread mass of four digits in height, on a base of 20 to 25 degrees, and like a parabola in the general outline, which was, however, broken up on the outer side into jets. Another broad sheet sprang up on the north-east (toward the zenith) nearly rectangular in shape, and three to four digits high, the upper third part being divided irregularly into tongues of light, formed by assemblages of rays. Between these larger masses the circumference of the lunar orb was filled up by radiate lines of brilliant light, extending on an average a digit and a half in height, or 125,000 miles from the sun's surface. It was noticeable that this continuous band was the most narrow on the lower left hand side (southwest by south) averaging about two-thirds of the width elsewhere, and was badly broken on its entire outline, as if the regularity were interfered with by the action of the string of bead-like protuberances jutting up through the interior portion of its volume.

The full amount of this irregularity was not perceptible with the naked eye, but the general distribution of long and short rays was the same. To the unaided vision the narrower portions of the corona were visible and bright; but the tongue-like extensions faded out into nothingness, whereas the telescope gave a definite outline all around, except at the summit of the first-named protrusion. We do not claim that the relative lengths of the different portions were exactly as laid down here; they were estimated at the instant, and transferred to paper directly; but the time allowed for observation (less than three minutes) was so short that it can scarcely be considered possible to reproduce every part of the outline with unfailing accuracy.

As stated in the letters from Des Moines, the images of the corona taken in the camera by Dr. Curtis, of the United States Navy, do not show so great a breadth of outline as is here represented, probably for the reason that the light of the outer portions was too faint, by comparison, to fix an image on the plate, while the more brilliant portions were burning their impress on the apparatus. The photographs show the corona to be least broad in the region of the protuberances, and have preserved the impress of as much of its breadth as corresponds to a distance of 105,000 miles from the sun's body, whence we may conclude that the photosphere extends to at least that distance, while the observations of Prof. Lane show that at three-fourths of that distance it possesses enough of illuminating power to light up the moon's surface to an extent sufficient to cause a reflection of its rays through a distance of 225,000 miles.

A legitimate conclusion from this, and through spectroscopic observations detailed in our reports, is that the solid body of the sun is surrounded by a self-luminous atmosphere of at least one hundred thousand miles in thickness, or one-fourth part of his radius, this giving the image fixed in the camera, and that outside of the light (photosphere is a non-luminous envelope or atmosphere, shining to us by means of the light received from the interior shell, which it reflects to our eyes. This non-luminous envelope or atmosphere, must be at least 600,000 miles in thickness, and perhaps twice that amount, as its density must decrease with the distance till it loses its reflective power. It is not impossible that the prolongation in the direction C A B, gives rise to the phenomenon known as the Zodiacal light; and rises sufficiently near the orbit of Mercury to cause the disturbances in his movements which have been ascribed to a mythical belt of planetoids.

These are represented on the diagram in black; their apparent color was a pink red. The instant that the last thin film of light, with its middle at D, had vanished, leaving the sun in utter darkness, and simultaneously with the outflash of the corona, the line of protuberances extending from P to B also burst upon the view. The one at the lowest point was the largest. All saw the upper portion, which occupied about 16 degrees on the moon's disc, and projected 56,000 miles from the sun's edge, or fully one-half the average height of the photosphere. Dr. Hilgard saw and described the lower, or pendant portion, which was estimated to be 100,000 miles long, by 20,000 miles wide, making a total protrusion of 156,000 miles. The protuberance at L, and the one immediately below it, were also visible to the naked eye; they were rectangular, and were estimated at 20,000 miles high, with bases of five and eight degrees on the circumference. The photograph showed the three more fancifully-shaped ones near the eastern quarter, which were also more faint in outline, seeming as if one part lay far behind the other, which crosses it in the diagram. Hence the cross-shaped figure at B was probably made up of two independent protuberances, the horizontal portion lying several hundred miles farther from the eye of the spectator than the part which seemed to stand nearly upright. In the lower-left quarter a string of bead-like protuberances were also visible with the aid of the telescope. Their comparative size is necessarily exaggerated on our diagram; they were, perhaps, not more than 5,000 miles high, and dropped out of sight in rapid succession in a few seconds, as the moon advanced rapidly in the direction C to D. And now the three larger ones at D, B grew smaller, fading from the view about the middle of totality, which fact showed them to have an altitude of about 25,000 miles.

At this time the western edge of the moon had advanced sufficiently in its course to uncover the protuberances on that side, and the three shown from A to R flashed on the vision, only the exterior portions being visible at first, but soon growing out farther and farther till the three exhibited an altitude of at least 20,000 miles, by an aggregate breadth of fully 20 degrees on the base. Meanwhile the protuberance at P grew larger, unsteadily, as the moon's edge at that point neared the edge of the sun, but it then seemed to decrease shortly before the total phase ended, showing an actual change in volume, though the character of the outlines did not perceptibly vary. These four were distinctly visible till the last instant, when they vanished with the corona, as a star disappears from the view when a flash of lightning illumines the firmament.

The spectroscope had already told us that these protuberances are masses of incandescent matter, and some of its constituent elements have been determined to be identical with substances peculiar to us, as iron, sodium, magnesium and hydrogen. But it was reserved to Professor Harkness to discover that there is a constant decrease in the number of elements in proportion to the height above the sun's surface. Thus the summit contains no element but hydrogen, and sodium appears a little lower, while iron is, possibly, the element to rise with the greatest difficulty, and to fall back soonest into the bosom of the sun. We have also reason to believe that these protuberances are identical with the dark masses known as "spots" when seen on that part of the sun's atmosphere which is between us and his body.

So much, then, we know of the constitution of the sun that he is surrounded by a double atmosphere, and that the interior one is self-luminous and the scene of violent changes connected with the formation and movement of immense bulks of incandescent matter. We know, further, that many of the substances which are found in large quantities on the earth exist also in the sun, and we may reason from analogy that other yet undiscovered terrene elements join these to make up the grand total of solar matter. But beyond this lies a vast void belonging to the regions of the unknown; probably much that will forever remain "unknowable" by mortals. But where knowledge ends speculation begins.

It has been thought that the lumin-luminous and non-luminous atmospheres of the sun are like two air strata in our atmosphere; not absolutely separable, nor divided by a line the position of which can be indicated. This is, we believe, the general theory with those who entertain one, that it is but a general distinction, like the discrimination between upper and lower portions of our atmosphere, the one merging into the other by imperceptible gradations, and the self-luminosity ceasing only when the density becomes too small to admit of that intensity of vibration which is supposed necessary to originate the sensation of light.

This may be so, but it seems quite as probable that the sun's condition is similar, in respect to form, with that of the earth before the continents were upheaved by volcanic force. Then the ocean covered the land, and was itself surrounded by an outer atmosphere of air, the two oceans, then as now, not only balancing each other, but being mutually necessary to the integrity of character pertaining to each. Of course it is not necessary that the photosphere should be composed of anything like what we call water, and indeed we have no particular reason to believe that oxygen, the chief constituent of water, is present at all. But it is necessarily a somewhat dense fluid, and is probably in a state of more intense motion than any intermovement of particles of which we have any knowledge. There is no doubt that this fluid is also intensely hot, but that is probably not a result of c[…]ustion, and is more a consequence of its rapid motion than a necessary condition of heat in the solar rays. So far as we know, light and heat are phenomenal only—mere conditions, not material entities—and these sensations are communicated only by the intermediate vibrations of material particles. It is always cold on the tops of high mountains, though there be level enough to admit of a large amount of earth radiation, and we must conclude that the difference is principally due to a lessened density of the atmosphere, which presents fewer particles to be vibrated in the passage of the solar rays; hence less of motion; hence less of the sensation of heat. The sun's rays are warm and light to us only because they vibrate through certain media. Take away those media, and the sensation is absent.

We have every reason to believe that the earth and moon have existed under somewhat similar conditions to those now witnessed in the sun, with this probable difference that the earth has a comparative excess of oxygen, and the sun of hydrogen, while the moon is deficient in both of those elements. To this difference we may perhaps look for consolation against the fear that the sun will be burned out ultimately, and leave our posterity a thousand generations hence to die out of cold. The above view is perfectly consistent, too, with the idea that the sun may be a fit residence for animated beings, organized in adaptation to the situation, and enables us to drop the difficulty which meets us in the attempt to conceive of an eternally self-sustaining conflagration.
text.fr:
L'éclipse de Soleil de samedi dernier était visible dans tous les États-Unis et leurs Territoires, mais la vue de la magnifique couronne qui entourait le Soleil n'était offerte qu'à ceux qui se trouvaient sur l'étroite bande de 156,4 miles de largeur balayée par l'ombre de la Lune. La lumière du Soleil est si puissante et si écrasante qu'elle masque le déploiement de la couronne à ceux qui sont situés à quelques yards seulement hors des limites de la totalité, bien qu'ils ne pussent discerner qu'un simple fil de lumière solaire au moment de la plus grande obscuration.

Pour l'information de ceux qui n'ont pas eu le privilège de voir le phénomène en raison de leur situation, comme de ceux qui ne l'ont vu qu'à l'œil nu dans la bande de totalité, nous présentons ici une vue de la couronne, telle que l'auteur l'a vue à Des Moines, dans l'Iowa, à travers un télescope, dessinée par lui immédiatement après le passage de l'obscuration totale, puis soumise à plusieurs des observateurs scientifiques présents, qui tous l'ont reconnue pour un portrait exact. La gravure montre aussi les protubérances de couleur rose, dont les plus grandes furent vues par lui, mais pour les positions des plus petites, et pour la description exacte de toutes, il est en partie redevable à d'autres, qui en avaient fait l'objet spécial de leur observation, tandis qu'il dirigeait son attention sur la couronne, pendant les 172¾ secondes qui s'écoulèrent entre les contacts apparents des bords est et ouest des deux astres.

La figure circulaire du diagramme ci-joint représente la Lune, dont la face sombre est tournée vers l'observateur. Bien que son diamètre réel soit 394 fois moindre que celui du Soleil, elle est cependant tellement plus proche de nous que, au moment de l'éclipse, son diamètre apparent était à celui du Soleil comme 21 est à 20, de sorte que le Soleil fut totalement obscurci pendant les 2 minutes 52¾ secondes qu'il lui fallut pour parcourir un espace égal à un vingtième du diamètre du Soleil. Le mouvement apparent de son centre suivait la ligne C à D, tandis que la trajectoire apparente du centre du Soleil peut être représentée par la ligne B à A, et la direction des pôles nord et sud du ciel par les points marqués N et S. La lettre Z représente la direction du zénith ; les lettres R et L, la direction de la droite et de la gauche. Il ressort clairement du diagramme que R était à peu près dans la direction du nord-ouest ; Z, à peu près du nord-est, et L, à peu près du sud-est.

Que les rayons de couleur claire et les protubérances sombres de couleur rose (ces dernières représentées par des taches noires sur le diagramme) appartenaient au Soleil et non à la Lune, cela ressort clairement du fait que, lorsque les bords du Soleil et de la Lune coïncidaient en D, au premier instant de l'obscuration totale, le bord de la Lune empiétant à quelque distance sur le Soleil en C, les protubérances du côté supérieur gauche étaient visibles, et la couronne de ce côté était plus grande, tandis que, lorsque la Lune eut avancé de sorte que les bords se joignaient presque en C, et que la Lune empiétait en D, les protubérances du côté D étaient invisibles, alors que celles du côté C apparaissaient, et que la couronne de ce dernier côté était la plus grande. En acceptant cette vue, nous obtenons une jauge de dimension qui nous permet de mesurer approximativement les dimensions des diverses parties de la couronne et des protubérances.

Ainsi : le Soleil sous-tend, comme on le sait, un diamètre réel de 851 736 miles, tandis que son diamètre angulaire apparent au moment de l'éclipse était de 31 minutes, 37,6 secondes d'espace, ce qui correspond à 412,76 miles par seconde, soit très près de 71 000 miles (70 979,66) par doigt, ou douzième du diamètre du Soleil. Mais pour trouver la quantité totale de projection, il est évident qu'il faut tenir compte non seulement de la quantité de saillie au-delà du bord de la Lune, mais aussi de celle qui est due au chevauchement du bord de la Lune au point et à l'instant de l'observation.

LA COURONNE.

La couronne différait remarquablement de toutes les idées préconçues sur le sujet, et de toutes les descriptions antérieures, tant par la taille que par la forme. On l'a toujours représentée comme presque annulaire (en forme d'anneau), d'une largeur à peu près égale tout autour du bord de la Lune, et n'excédant pas un dixième de son diamètre apparent. La couronne de samedi dernier était extrêmement irrégulière dans son contour, et en certains endroits se projetait jusqu'à une distance égale à la moitié entière du diamètre apparent de la Lune, soit près de 500 000 miles. Notre diagramme montre les longueurs relatives des diverses parties, sauf que sur les côtés la longueur est légèrement réduite par la largeur des filets de colonne.

La plus grande longueur était presque identique à la direction de la trajectoire de la Lune à travers la face du Soleil, laquelle coïncidait de très près avec le plan de l'écliptique. Du côté est (direction à partir de D) une masse de lumière jaillit jusqu'à la distance de cinq ou six doigts ; elle avait environ trente degrés de large à la base, et sa forme ressemblait presque à la moitié éloignée d'une feuille de peuplier blanc. Près de la Lune elle brillait d'une lumière blanche presque uniforme, mais en peu d'espace elle se brisait en rayons brillants, presque parallèles entre eux, et tous dirigés à peu près vers le centre du diagramme. Plus loin encore, ces rayons prenaient davantage un caractère strié, semblant reposer sur un fond plus sombre, et vers le sommet ils s'évanouissaient en une lumière plus diffuse et plus douce, quoique encore distincte et vive. Près de l'extrémité elle ressemblait davantage à un cumulus, mais la direction centrale des rayons restait nettement visible. Elle se fondait dans le fond d'azur presque imperceptiblement, mais le contour était parfait, sauf à l'extrême bout de la masse en forme de feuille. De l'autre côté du disque (direction à partir de A, C) se trouvait une langue correspondante, mais moins régulière, et ne s'étendant dans le vide que sur environ les deux tiers de cette longueur. Cette partie était plus brillante près de la base que sa contrepartie, et se terminait par un contour net à l'extrême bout, les rayons se mêlant si étroitement qu'il fallait un regard fixe pour les distinguer. L'étendue de cette partie était d'environ 255 000 miles. Le professeur Lane vit la lumière réfléchie par le bord de la Lune à la distance de 54 000 miles du corps du Soleil, tandis que la lumière était réfléchie par l'autre bord à une distance de 74 000 miles. Nous calculons la largeur totale de la couronne dans la direction passant par A D, y compris le corps du Soleil, à 1 600 000 miles.

La masse de lumière coronale la plus large était visible à gauche (dans le quart sud-est). Elle partait d'un arc d'environ 50 degrés de la circonférence de la Lune, jusqu'à une hauteur de trois doigts, soit 224 000 miles. Cette masse était plus diffuse que chacune des autres, et se séparait près de l'extrémité en feuillets étroits de lumière, un peu comme la flamme d'un lit de charbons clairsemé, sauf qu'il n'y avait pas de rouge, la lumière étant d'un blanc pur, avec une faible coruscation. À l'opposé, à droite, se trouvait une autre masse étalée en feuille, de quatre doigts de hauteur, sur une base de 20 à 25 degrés, et semblable à une parabole dans son contour général, qui était cependant brisé du côté extérieur en jets. Une autre large nappe s'élevait au nord-est (vers le zénith), de forme presque rectangulaire, haute de trois à quatre doigts, le tiers supérieur étant divisé irrégulièrement en langues de lumière, formées par des assemblages de rayons. Entre ces masses plus grandes, la circonférence du globe lunaire était remplie de lignes rayonnantes de lumière brillante, s'étendant en moyenne sur un doigt et demi de hauteur, soit 125 000 miles depuis la surface du Soleil. On remarquait que cette bande continue était la plus étroite du côté inférieur gauche (sud-ouest quart sud), atteignant en moyenne environ les deux tiers de la largeur ailleurs, et qu'elle était fortement brisée sur tout son contour, comme si la régularité était troublée par l'action de la file de protubérances en forme de perles qui surgissaient à travers la partie intérieure de son volume.

Toute l'étendue de cette irrégularité n'était pas perceptible à l'œil nu, mais la distribution générale des rayons longs et courts était la même. À la vue non aidée, les parties plus étroites de la couronne étaient visibles et brillantes ; mais les prolongements en forme de langues s'évanouissaient dans le néant, alors que le télescope donnait un contour défini tout autour, sauf au sommet de la première saillie nommée. Nous ne prétendons pas que les longueurs relatives des différentes parties fussent exactement telles qu'elles sont tracées ici ; elles ont été estimées sur l'instant, et reportées directement sur le papier ; mais le temps accordé à l'observation (moins de trois minutes) était si court qu'on peut à peine juger possible de reproduire chaque partie du contour avec une exactitude infaillible.

Comme il est dit dans les lettres de Des Moines, les images de la couronne prises dans la chambre noire par le docteur Curtis, de la marine des États-Unis, ne montrent pas un contour d'une largeur aussi grande que celle qui est représentée ici, probablement parce que la lumière des parties extérieures était trop faible, par comparaison, pour fixer une image sur la plaque, tandis que les parties plus brillantes imprimaient leur marque sur l'appareil. Les photographies montrent que la couronne est la moins large dans la région des protubérances, et ont conservé l'empreinte d'autant de sa largeur qu'il en correspond à une distance de 105 000 miles du corps du Soleil, d'où nous pouvons conclure que la photosphère s'étend au moins jusqu'à cette distance, tandis que les observations du professeur Lane montrent qu'aux trois quarts de cette distance elle possède assez de pouvoir éclairant pour illuminer la surface de la Lune à un degré suffisant pour causer une réflexion de ses rayons à travers une distance de 225 000 miles.

Une conclusion légitime à tirer de cela, et des observations spectroscopiques détaillées dans nos rapports, est que le corps solide du Soleil est entouré d'une atmosphère lumineuse par elle-même d'au moins cent mille miles d'épaisseur, soit un quart de son rayon, ce qui donne l'image fixée dans la chambre noire, et qu'en dehors de la lumière (photosphère est une enveloppe ou atmosphère non lumineuse, brillant pour nous au moyen de la lumière reçue de la couche intérieure, qu'elle réfléchit vers nos yeux. Cette enveloppe ou atmosphère non lumineuse doit avoir au moins 600 000 miles d'épaisseur, et peut-être le double, car sa densité doit décroître avec la distance jusqu'à perdre son pouvoir réfléchissant. Il n'est pas impossible que le prolongement dans la direction C A B donne naissance au phénomène connu sous le nom de lumière zodiacale ; et s'élève assez près de l'orbite de Mercure pour causer les perturbations de ses mouvements qu'on a attribuées à une ceinture mythique de planétoïdes.

Elles sont représentées en noir sur le diagramme ; leur couleur apparente était un rouge rosé. À l'instant où la dernière mince pellicule de lumière, dont le milieu était en D, eut disparu, laissant le Soleil dans une obscurité complète, et simultanément avec l'éclat soudain de la couronne, la ligne de protubérances s'étendant de P à B se montra aussi soudain à la vue. Celle du point le plus bas était la plus grande. Tous virent la partie supérieure, qui occupait environ 16 degrés sur le disque de la Lune, et se projetait à 56 000 miles du bord du Soleil, soit pleinement la moitié de la hauteur moyenne de la photosphère. Le docteur Hilgard vit et décrivit la partie inférieure, ou pendante, qu'on estima longue de 100 000 miles, sur 20 000 miles de large, ce qui donne une saillie totale de 156 000 miles. La protubérance en L, et celle qui est immédiatement au-dessous, étaient aussi visibles à l'œil nu ; elles étaient rectangulaires, et on les estima à 20 000 miles de haut, avec des bases de cinq et de huit degrés sur la circonférence. La photographie montra les trois plus fantaisistes de forme près du quart oriental, qui étaient aussi plus faibles de contour, paraissant comme si une partie se trouvait loin derrière l'autre, qui la croise dans le diagramme. De là, la figure en croix en B était probablement composée de deux protubérances indépendantes, la partie horizontale se trouvant plusieurs centaines de miles plus loin de l'œil du spectateur que la partie qui semblait se tenir presque droite. Dans le quart inférieur gauche, une file de protubérances en forme de perles était aussi visible à l'aide du télescope. Leur taille comparative est nécessairement exagérée sur notre diagramme ; elles n'avaient peut-être pas plus de 5 000 miles de haut, et disparurent à la vue en succession rapide en quelques secondes, tandis que la Lune avançait rapidement dans la direction C à D. Et maintenant les trois plus grandes en D, B diminuèrent, s'effaçant de la vue vers le milieu de la totalité, ce qui montra qu'elles avaient une altitude d'environ 25 000 miles.

À ce moment, le bord occidental de la Lune avait suffisamment avancé dans sa course pour découvrir les protubérances de ce côté, et les trois qui sont montrées de A à R jaillirent à la vue, seules les parties extérieures étant d'abord visibles, mais bientôt elles se développèrent de plus en plus loin jusqu'à ce que les trois présentassent une altitude d'au moins 20 000 miles, pour une largeur totale de pleinement 20 degrés à la base. Pendant ce temps, la protubérance en P grossit, de façon irrégulière, à mesure que le bord de la Lune en ce point approchait du bord du Soleil, mais elle sembla ensuite diminuer peu avant la fin de la phase totale, montrant un changement réel de volume, bien que le caractère des contours ne variât pas de façon perceptible. Ces quatre restèrent distinctement visibles jusqu'au dernier instant, où elles disparurent avec la couronne, comme une étoile disparaît de la vue lorsqu'un éclair illumine le firmament.

Le spectroscope nous avait déjà appris que ces protubérances sont des masses de matière incandescente, et l'on a déterminé que certains de ses éléments constitutifs sont identiques à des substances qui nous sont propres, comme le fer, le sodium, le magnésium et l'hydrogène. Mais il était réservé au professeur Harkness de découvrir qu'il y a une diminution constante du nombre d'éléments à proportion de la hauteur au-dessus de la surface du Soleil. Ainsi le sommet ne contient aucun élément sauf l'hydrogène, et le sodium apparaît un peu plus bas, tandis que le fer est, peut-être, l'élément qui s'élève avec le plus de difficulté, et retombe le plus tôt dans le sein du Soleil. Nous avons aussi lieu de croire que ces protubérances sont identiques aux masses sombres connues sous le nom de « taches » lorsqu'on les voit sur la partie de l'atmosphère du Soleil qui se trouve entre nous et son corps.

Voilà donc ce que nous savons de la constitution du Soleil : il est entouré d'une double atmosphère, et l'atmosphère intérieure est lumineuse par elle-même et le théâtre de changements violents liés à la formation et au mouvement d'immenses masses de matière incandescente. Nous savons, de plus, que bon nombre des substances qu'on trouve en grande quantité sur la Terre existent aussi dans le Soleil, et nous pouvons raisonner par analogie que d'autres éléments terrestres encore non découverts se joignent à ceux-ci pour composer le grand total de la matière solaire. Mais au-delà s'étend un vaste vide appartenant aux régions de l'inconnu ; probablement beaucoup de ce qui restera à jamais « inconnaissable » pour les mortels. Mais là où finit la connaissance commence la spéculation.

On a pensé que les atmosphères lumineuse et non lumineuse du Soleil sont comme deux couches d'air de notre atmosphère ; non absolument séparables, ni divisées par une ligne dont on puisse indiquer la position. C'est, croyons-nous, la théorie générale chez ceux qui en entretiennent une, que ce n'est qu'une distinction générale, comme la distinction entre les parties supérieure et inférieure de notre atmosphère, l'une se fondant dans l'autre par des gradations imperceptibles, et la luminosité propre ne cessant que lorsque la densité devient trop faible pour admettre cette intensité de vibration qu'on suppose nécessaire pour engendrer la sensation de lumière.

Cela peut être, mais il paraît tout aussi probable que l'état du Soleil est semblable, quant à la forme, à celui de la Terre avant que les continents fussent soulevés par la force volcanique. Alors l'océan couvrait la terre, et était lui-même entouré d'une atmosphère extérieure d'air, les deux océans, alors comme maintenant, non seulement s'équilibrant l'un l'autre, mais étant mutuellement nécessaires à l'intégrité de caractère propre à chacun. Il n'est bien sûr pas nécessaire que la photosphère soit composée de quoi que ce soit de semblable à ce que nous appelons l'eau, et en vérité nous n'avons aucune raison particulière de croire que l'oxygène, constituant principal de l'eau, y soit présent le moins du monde. Mais c'est nécessairement un fluide quelque peu dense, et il est probablement dans un état de mouvement plus intense que tout mouvement mutuel de particules dont nous ayons connaissance. Il n'est pas douteux que ce fluide est aussi intensément chaud, mais ce n'est probablement pas un résultat de la c[…]ustion, et c'est plus une conséquence de son mouvement rapide qu'une condition nécessaire de la chaleur dans les rayons solaires. Autant que nous le sachions, la lumière et la chaleur ne sont que phénoménales — de simples conditions, non des entités matérielles — et ces sensations ne sont communiquées que par les vibrations intermédiaires de particules matérielles. Il fait toujours froid au sommet des hautes montagnes, bien qu'il y ait assez de plaine pour admettre une grande quantité de rayonnement du sol, et nous devons conclure que la différence est principalement due à une moindre densité de l'atmosphère, qui présente moins de particules à faire vibrer au passage des rayons solaires ; donc moins de mouvement ; donc moins de sensation de chaleur. Les rayons du Soleil ne sont chauds et lumineux pour nous que parce qu'ils vibrent à travers certains milieux. Retirez ces milieux, et la sensation est absente.

Nous avons toute raison de croire que la Terre et la Lune ont existé dans des conditions quelque peu semblables à celles que l'on constate maintenant dans le Soleil, avec cette différence probable que la Terre a un excès relatif d'oxygène, et le Soleil d'hydrogène, tandis que la Lune est déficiente en ces deux éléments. De cette différence nous pouvons peut-être tirer consolation contre la crainte que le Soleil ne s'épuise finalement en brûlant, et ne laisse nos descendants, mille générations plus tard, mourir de froid. La vue ci-dessus est aussi parfaitement conforme à l'idée que le Soleil puisse être une demeure convenable pour des êtres animés, organisés en adaptation à la situation, et nous permet d'écarter la difficulté qui se présente à nous lorsque nous tentons de concevoir un incendie qui s'entretient éternellement de lui-même.
text.es:
El eclipse de Sol del sábado pasado fue visible en todos los Estados Unidos y sus Territorios, pero la vista de la magnífica corona que rodeaba al Sol solo la tuvieron quienes se encontraban en la estrecha franja de 156,4 millas de ancho que barrió la sombra de la Luna. La luz del Sol es tan potente y tan abrumadora que oculta el espectáculo de la corona a quienes se hallan situados apenas unas yardas fuera de los límites de la totalidad, aunque estos podían distinguir un simple hilo de luz solar en el momento de mayor oscurecimiento.

Para información de quienes no tuvieron el privilegio de presenciar el fenómeno por razón de su situación, así como de quienes solo lo vieron a simple vista dentro de la banda de totalidad, presentamos aquí una vista de la corona, tal como la vio en Des Moines, Iowa, quien escribe, con un telescopio; la dibujó inmediatamente después de pasada la obscuración total y luego la sometió a varios de los observadores científicos presentes, todos los cuales la reconocieron como un retrato exacto. El grabado muestra también las protuberancias de color rosa, de las cuales vio él las mayores; pero en cuanto a las posiciones de las menores y a la descripción exacta de todas, está en parte en deuda con otros, que las tomaron como objeto especial de observación mientras él dirigía su atención a la corona, durante los 172¾ segundos que transcurrieron entre los contactos aparentes de los bordes oriental y occidental de los astros.

La figura circular del diagrama adjunto representa la Luna, con su lado oscuro vuelto hacia el observador. Aunque su diámetro real es 394 veces menor que el del Sol, está tanto más cerca de nosotros que, en el momento del eclipse, su diámetro aparente era al del Sol como 21 a 20, de modo que el Sol quedó totalmente oscurecido durante los 2 minutos 52¾ segundos que ella necesitó para recorrer un espacio igual a la vigésima parte del diámetro del Sol. El movimiento aparente de su centro iba por la línea de C a D, mientras que la trayectoria aparente del centro del Sol puede representarse por la línea de B a A, y la dirección de los polos norte y sur del cielo, por los puntos marcados N y S. La letra Z representa la dirección del cenit; las letras R y L, la dirección de la derecha y de la izquierda. Del diagrama se ve con claridad que R estaba casi en dirección noroeste; Z, casi noreste, y L, casi sudeste.

Que los rayos de color claro y las protuberancias de color rosa oscuro (estas últimas representadas por manchas negras en el diagrama) pertenecían al Sol y no a la Luna, es evidente por el hecho de que, cuando los bordes del Sol y de la Luna coincidían en D, en el primer instante de obscuración total, con el borde de la Luna montándose cierta distancia sobre el Sol en C, eran visibles las protuberancias del lado superior izquierdo y la corona de ese lado era mayor; mientras que, cuando la Luna había avanzado de modo que los bordes casi se unían en C y la Luna se montaba sobre el Sol en D, las protuberancias del lado D eran invisibles, en tanto que las del lado C aparecían a la vista, y la corona de este último lado era la mayor. Aceptando este punto de vista obtenemos una medida de dimensión que nos permite medir aproximadamente las dimensiones de las diversas partes de la corona y de las protuberancias.

Así: se sabe que el Sol subtiende un diámetro real de 851.736 millas, mientras que su diámetro angular aparente en el momento del eclipse era de 31 minutos, 37,6 segundos de arco, lo que corresponde a 412,76 millas por cada segundo, o casi exactamente 71.000 millas (70.979,66) por cada dígito, o duodécima parte del diámetro del Sol. Pero para hallar la cantidad total de proyección, es evidente que debemos tomar en cuenta no solo la cantidad de protrusión más allá del borde de la Luna, sino también la debida al solapamiento del borde de la Luna en el punto y el instante de la observación.

LA CORONA.

La corona era notablemente distinta de todas las nociones preconcebidas sobre el asunto y de todas las descripciones anteriores, tanto en tamaño como en forma. Siempre se la ha representado casi anular (en forma de anillo), de una anchura aproximadamente igual en todo el borde de la Luna y no mayor que la décima parte de su diámetro aparente. La corona del sábado pasado era sumamente irregular en su contorno y en algunos lugares se proyectaba hasta una distancia de la mitad entera del diámetro aparente de la Luna, o casi 500.000 millas. Nuestro diagrama muestra las longitudes relativas de las diversas porciones, salvo que, en los lados, la longitud queda ligeramente comprimida por el ancho de los filetes de columna.

La mayor longitud coincidía casi por completo con la dirección de la trayectoria de la Luna a través del disco del Sol, que coincidía muy de cerca con el plano de la eclíptica. Del lado este (dirección desde D) salía disparada una masa de luz hasta la distancia de cinco o seis dígitos; tenía unos treinta grados de ancho en la base y la forma casi de la mitad lejana de una hoja de álamo blanco.
